Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious 'Search for perplexity ai' extension files written (ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd) · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Browser traffic to Perplexity look-alike domain perplexity-ai.online (search interception) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Browser traffic to Perplexity look-alike domain perplexity-ai.online (search interception) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts browser processes resolving or connecting to the attacker-controlled look-alike domain perplexity-ai[.]online, which the malicious 'Search for perplexity ai' extension uses as its search and suggest_url endpoint to log every query and every address-bar keystroke before redirecting to a real engine. Any contact to this domain is the data-theft hop itself. Rationale: Uses the exact attacker domain perplexity-ai[.]online named in the article as the search/suggest_url interception endpoint. The domain has no legitimate use, making any browser contact high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://windowsnews.ai/article/microsoft-flags-malicious-perplexity-ai-extension-stealing-search-traffic-on-windows.432081 • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1056.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or threat-intel enrichment host detonating the sample and resolving the domain
  • Security researcher manually browsing the IOC for triage
  • Passive-DNS / TI scanner resolving the domain for reputation lookups
  • DNS sinkhole or secure web gateway pre-resolving blocked domains for logging
  • A user who manually visited a write-up that hot-links the live domain
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("sandbox01","malware-detonation","ti-enrich01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm which host/user and which browser process generated the contact; pull DeviceInfo.LoggedOnUsers and check whether the default search engine was changed. 2) Contain: Block perplexity-ai[.]online at the proxy/DNS, isolate the host if the extension is still present, and force-remove the 'Search for perplexity ai' extension (ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd). 3) Hunt: Pivot org-wide on the domain and the extension ID across DeviceFileEvents/DeviceNetworkEvents to scope every affected endpoint; review proxy logs for the volume of suggest_url beacons (one per keystroke) to gauge data captured.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "perplexity-ai.online"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "perplexity-ai.online"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Query to Malicious Perplexity Look-alike Domain perplexity-ai.online
id: 7c3f1d8e-9b2a-4e6c-a1f0-2d5b8c4a9e11
description: Detects DNS resolution of perplexity-ai.online, the attacker C2/logging domain used by the malicious 'Search for perplexity ai' Chrome extension to intercept searches and address-bar input.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1041
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|contains: 'perplexity-ai.online'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:*perplexity-ai.online*
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/perplexity-ai\.online/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query="*perplexity-ai.online*" by DNS.src, DNS.dest, DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query="*perplexity-ai.online*" by DNS.src, DNS.dest, DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Malicious 'Search for perplexity ai' extension files written (ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd) AIInstallation High
Hunts on-disk installation of the specific malicious Chrome/Edge extension by its store ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd, which Chromium writes under the browser profile's \Extensions\<id>\ folder. Catches the install/persistence step even on hosts where the extension was sideloaded after Google's store takedown. Rationale: Uses the exact Chrome Web Store extension ID (flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd) confirmed in the article and the store URL; Chromium materializes this ID in the on-disk \Extensions\<id>\ path, so a file-path match is a unique, low-FP installation signal. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd
ATT&CKT1176 T1204.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic/IR tooling copying or imaging a browser profile that already contained the extension
  • EDR sample-collection job archiving the extension folder for analysis
  • Backup/sync agent (OneDrive, roaming profile) replicating the leftover extension directory
  • Analyst intentionally reinstalling the sample in a controlled VM
  • Chrome profile migration tools moving an old profile between hosts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","robocopy.exe","onedrive.exe","backup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the host/user and the InitiatingProcess that wrote the files; check whether chrome.exe/msedge.exe was the writer (live install) vs a backup/IR tool. 2) Contain: Remove the extension via browser policy (force-uninstall ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd), reset the default search engine, and block perplexity-ai[.]online. 3) Hunt: Correlate with UC1 network hits to confirm the extension actually beaconed; sweep the fleet for the same extension ID and any other AI-branded extensions with declarativeNetRequest permissions installed in the same window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-29 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious Chromium-based extension that spoofs the AI-powered answer engine Perplexity AI redirects browser search traffic using MV3 APIs and intermediary infrastructure. The post Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious Perplexity-spoofing extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to disk · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Search-interception traffic to Perplexity typosquat domain perplexity-ai[.]online · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Search-interception traffic to Perplexity typosquat domain perplexity-ai[.]online AICommand & Control High
Hunts browser connections/DNS resolutions to the attacker-controlled search-interception infrastructure (perplexity-ai.online and related oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws) used by the fake 'Search for perplexity ai' Chromium extension. Because the extension routes every Omnibox query and keystroke-level suggestion through this domain before redirecting to a real engine, any browser-originated traffic to these hosts is high-fidelity evidence of an infected endpoint. Rationale: Anchored on the exact interception domain perplexity-ai.online (confirmed by both the MSFT blog and The Hacker News) plus the pre-extracted secondary infra oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws, scoped to browser parent processes — a typosquat domain reached by a browser is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/search-for-perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd • https://www.crx4chrome.com/extensions/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176 T1185
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/IR analyst detonating the extension sample in a managed sandbox host
  • Web proxy / secure-web-gateway pre-fetching or URL-categorizing the domain on a user's behalf
  • Threat-intel enrichment or DNS-sinkhole tooling resolving the IOC for blocking
  • A user who clicked the lookalike landing page once but did not install (single browse vs. repeated query routing)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which device/user generated the traffic and whether the 'Search for perplexity ai' extension (ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd) is installed; check if default search provider was overridden to perplexity-ai.online. 2) Contain: force-remove the extension via browser policy/ExtensionInstallBlocklist, reset the default search engine, and block perplexity-ai.online / oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws at proxy and DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on all other hosts resolving these domains and review browsing/search history routed through the domain for sensitive query exposure during the exposure window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","chrome_proxy.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Query to Perplexity Typosquat Search-Interception Domain
id: 5b3e9a42-7c1f-4d2a-9f6e-2a1c8d4b7e90
description: Detects DNS resolution of perplexity-ai.online and related infrastructure used by a malicious Chromium extension spoofing Perplexity AI to intercept browser search queries.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/29/chromium-extension-uses-airelated-branding-redirect-browser-search/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/29
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1176
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|contains:
      - perplexity-ai.online
      - oda.digital
      - extension.tilda.ws
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*perplexity-ai.online* OR *oda.digital* OR extension.tilda.ws)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(perplexity-ai\.online|oda\.digital|extension\.tilda\.ws)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*perplexity-ai.online*" OR DNS.query="*oda.digital*" OR DNS.query="extension.tilda.ws") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*perplexity-ai.online*" OR DNS.query="*oda.digital*" OR DNS.query="extension.tilda.ws") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Malicious Perplexity-spoofing extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to disk AIInstallation High
Hunts for the unique Chrome Web Store extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd ('Search for perplexity ai') appearing in browser extension folder paths or written files on managed endpoints. The extension ID is a globally unique 32-char identifier, so any file-system artifact bearing it is a deterministic indicator that the taken-down malicious search hijacker was installed. Rationale: The 32-char extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd is a globally unique store identifier (confirmed via the Chrome Web Store and crx4chrome listings), so its presence in any extension folder path is a deterministic install indicator with effectively no collisions. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/search-for-perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd • https://www.crx4chrome.com/extensions/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd/
ATT&CKT1176 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup software capturing the Chrome 'User Data' profile directory that still contains the extension folder
  • IR/forensic collection tooling copying browser profiles for offline analysis
  • AV/EDR scanning or quarantining the extension folder (file-access touches the path)
  • Sync of an already-infected profile to a new device via Chrome profile sync before takedown
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the ActionType (FileCreated = fresh install vs FileDeleted = remediation) and identify the user profile and browser hosting the extension folder. 2) Contain: remove the extension, push it to the browser ExtensionInstallBlocklist policy, and reset the hijacked default search provider; block perplexity-ai.online at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 network telemetry to confirm queries were exfiltrated, and sweep the fleet for the same extension ID to find all installs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'

            - '\cmd.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'

UNC5792/UNC4221 Signal & WhatsApp typosquat lure-domain resolution AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network resolutions to the specific Signal/WhatsApp lookalike domains used by Russian-linked UNC5792/UNC4221 to host fake group-invite and 2FA pages. Article-specific because it pins the exact actor-controlled typosquat domain list rather than a generic 'phishing domain' heuristic. Rationale: Uses the exact UNC5792/UNC4221 typosquat domain list (signal-group*, *-signal*, signal-security*, signal-device-off*) cross-checked against the FBI/CISA IC3 PSA I-062626 and Google/Mandiant 'Signals of Trouble' report; named IOC domains make this high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260626 • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/russia-targeting-signal-messenger/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-russian-hackers-now-target-signal-backup-recovery-keys/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing the IOC domains in an isolated VM/sandbox
  • EDR/SOAR automated URL detonation resolving the domains during enrichment
  • Security proxy or DNS sinkhole resolving the domains to a block page
  • A targeted user who clicked the lure to 'investigate' and self-reported
  • Threat-feed enrichment service pre-resolving submitted IOCs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","SenseSampleUploader.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the device/user that resolved the domain and the initiating process (browser vs. tooling); confirm it is a real user and not a sandbox/proxy host. 2) Contain: block all 20 typosquat domains at proxy/DNS, force-reset the user's Signal/messaging session, and instruct the user to open Signal > Linked Devices and remove unknown devices and rotate the backup recovery key. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same device/user for the sgnl://linkdevice URI (UC3) and inbound mail/DMs from fake 'Signal support' accounts; sweep the org for any other host resolving these domains.

Inbound mail delivering UNC5792 Signal recovery-key lure domains AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound email whose embedded URLs point to the UNC5792/UNC4221 Signal/WhatsApp typosquat domains. Although the campaign primarily uses in-app DMs, the same actor domains are also distributed via email; this surfaces delivery to mailboxes of high-value targets. Rationale: Joins EmailEvents to EmailUrlInfo on the exact actor typosquat domains so only mail carrying a UNC5792 lure URL fires; sender impersonation of 'Signal support' plus a typosquat link is high-fidelity. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/Splunk left empty because EmailUrlInfo has no equivalent in those telemetry sets (mail-flow URL data lives only in Defender XDR for this tenant). Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260626 • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/russia-targeting-signal-messenger/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal phishing-simulation platform using look-alike domains for training
  • A user forwarding a reported phishing email internally (inbound to the SOC mailbox)
  • Threat-intel newsletter or vendor advisory email quoting the IOC domains as text/links
  • Security awareness team distributing screenshots of the lure with the domain visible
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourphishingsim-vendor.com" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the message is external/inbound and the URL host is one of the actor domains (not a quoted IOC in an advisory); check DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation to see if it reached the inbox. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message tenant-wide via the NetworkMessageId, block the sender and domains, and check UrlClickEvents for whether the recipient clicked. 3) Hunt: if clicked, pivot the recipient to UC1 (domain resolution) and UC3 (device-link URI), and review the user's Signal linked devices and recovery-key status.

Signal linked-device hijack URI (sgnl://linkdevice) & recovery-key lure pages AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the UNC5792 device-linking abuse signature — the sgnl://linkdevice?uuid= deep-link Mandiant documented in fake Signal group-invite pages — plus web-proxy hits to the recovery-key/2FA harvest domains. This is the actual account-takeover mechanism, distinct from generic domain resolution. Rationale: Pivots on the Mandiant-documented sgnl://linkdevice?uuid= device-linking URI (the persistent-eavesdrop mechanism) and the credential-harvest domain subset (signal-security*, signal-device-off*, *-confirm*) tied to the recovery-key/2FA ruse; both cross-checked against Google/Mandiant and IC3 PSA. Confidence Medium because deep-link capture depends on full-URL proxy/command-line telemetry being present. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/russia-targeting-signal-messenger/ • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260626
ATT&CKT1621 T1111 T1656
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user genuinely linking a second Signal desktop/iPad via an official sgnl://linkdevice link
  • QA/IT testing of Signal desktop provisioning on managed devices
  • Security researcher reproducing the Mandiant device-link PoC in a lab
  • Proxy logging an official signal.org-hosted link rendered with the same scheme
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has "sgnl://linkdevice" and (RemoteUrl has "signal.org" or RemoteUrl has "//signal.me/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the sgnl://linkdevice URI / lure-domain hit originated from an official Signal flow (signal.org) or from one of the actor typosquat domains; identify the user and host. 2) Contain: instruct the user to open Signal > Linked Devices, remove any unrecognized linked device immediately, rotate the backup recovery key, and re-register; block the credential-harvest domains. 3) Hunt: review the prior 7 days for the same user receiving 'Signal support' impersonation contact, resolutions to other typosquat domains (UC1), and any inbound mail lures (UC2); check for unusual message-history access on the account.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"

SimpleHelp RMM agent spawning script interpreters/LOLBins (CVE-2026-48558 trusted-channel execution) AIDelivery High
Hunts the SimpleHelp on-endpoint agent ('Remote Access'/'SimpleService' under the JWrapper-Remote Access folder) spawning script hosts or download LOLBins. After exploiting CVE-2026-48558 to mint a rogue Technician account, the operator drives the managed endpoint through the RMM to execute commands and transfer the TaskWeaver loader. Legitimate helpdesk use rarely launches wscript/node/curl from the agent. Rationale: Pivots on the SimpleHelp agent process/folder (Remote Access.exe / SimpleService.exe / JWrapper-Remote Access) as parent of script/download binaries — the article's 'trusted administrative channel transferring files and executing commands'. Cross-checked CVE detail against Horizon3.ai and Tenable. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-48558/ • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-48558 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/16/simplehelp-rmm-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1219 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk technician legitimately running a PowerShell/cmd remediation script through SimpleHelp
  • MSP automation pushing Node.js-based tooling via the agent
  • Software deployment using certutil/bitsadmin to fetch installers
  • Inventory scripts (wscript/cscript) run by an admin during a remote session
  • SimpleHelp self-update spawning a child process
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("-Update", "simplehelp", "\\Program Files\\") and AccountName in~ ("helpdesk","svc-rmm"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the SimpleHelp session was driven by a recognized Technician account; cross-reference SimpleHelp server logs for newly created OIDC technician accounts (CVE-2026-48558). Inspect the child command line for jquery.js or trycloudflare references. 2) Contain: invalidate unrecognized technician sessions, isolate the endpoint, and block the child process hash; if the account is rogue, disable it and patch SimpleHelp to 5.5.16/6.0 RC2. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for jquery.js execution, *.trycloudflare.com connections, and developer-credential file access (UC2-UC5).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "JWrapper-Remote Access" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Remote Access.exe","SimpleService.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe","mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has "JWrapper-Remote Access" or ParentProcessName has_any ("Remote Access.exe","SimpleService.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe","mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SimpleHelp RMM Agent Spawning Script Interpreter or Download LOLBin
id: 5f1b2c8a-9d44-4e2a-bb31-7c0e9a1f2d10
description: Detects the SimpleHelp endpoint agent spawning script hosts or download utilities, consistent with CVE-2026-48558 abuse to deploy TaskWeaver/Djinn.
references:

  - https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-48558/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/29
tags:
  - attack.t1219
  - attack.t1059
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|contains:
      - 'JWrapper-Remote Access'
      - '\Remote Access.exe'
      - '\SimpleService.exe'
  selection_child:

      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:(*Remote?Access.exe OR *SimpleService.exe OR *JWrapper-Remote?Access*)) @Image:(*wscript.exe OR *cscript.exe OR *node.exe OR *mshta.exe OR *powershell.exe OR *pwsh.exe OR *cmd.exe OR *curl.exe OR *bitsadmin.exe OR *certutil.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(Remote Access|SimpleService)\.exe$/i | ImageFileName=/(wscript|cscript|node|mshta|powershell|pwsh|cmd|curl|bitsadmin|certutil)\.exe$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("Remote Access.exe","SimpleService.exe") OR Processes.parent_process_path="*JWrapper-Remote Access*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe","mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("Remote Access.exe","SimpleService.exe") OR Processes.parent_process_path="*JWrapper-Remote Access*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe","mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
TaskWeaver loader: obfuscated 'jquery.js' executed by WSH/Node/MSHTA AIInstallation High
Hunts a script interpreter executing a file literally named jquery.js — the disguise TaskWeaver uses. The legitimate jQuery library is a browser asset and is never run through wscript/cscript/node/mshta on an endpoint, making this an extremely high-fidelity execution signal. Rationale: Uses the article's exact loader artifact: an obfuscated JavaScript file named 'jquery.js' run as TaskWeaver. Pairing a WSH/Node/MSHTA interpreter with a jquery.js argument is near-zero-FP because real jQuery never executes that way. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-critical-simplehelp-flaw-deploy-new-djinn-infostealer-taskweaver-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer deliberately running a Node.js script that happens to be named jquery.js
  • Build tooling minifying/processing a file path containing 'jquery.js' as an argument to node
  • Security testing/EDR validation replaying the artifact
  • An npm postinstall script referencing jquery.js by path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "node_modules" and ProcessCommandLine !has "npm"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the jquery.js file and its SHA256; deobfuscate or detonate to confirm fingerprinting/C2 behavior; check the parent (SimpleHelp agent? browser? email?). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the interpreter process tree, and quarantine jquery.js plus any modules it pulled. 3) Hunt: search the environment for the same SHA256, for *.trycloudflare.com beacons (UC3), and for subsequent developer-credential collection (UC4/UC5).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe","mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe","mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has "jquery.js"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Script interpreter beaconing to *.trycloudflare.com (TaskWeaver download/C2) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts WSH/Node/MSHTA/curl reaching an ephemeral Cloudflare Quick Tunnel domain (*.trycloudflare.com) — where TaskWeaver was hosted and where it pulls JavaScript modules. Tying the interpreter process to the tunnel domain removes generic CDN noise. Rationale: Article states jquery.js/TaskWeaver was downloaded from a 'temporary Cloudflare domain' and pulls further JS modules from C2. Scoping the trycloudflare lookup to script interpreters (not browsers) keeps fidelity; per the KB anti-pattern, trycloudflare is kept in-scope rather than allowlisted. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-critical-simplehelp-flaw-deploy-new-djinn-infostealer-taskweaver-malware/
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a legitimate Cloudflare Quick Tunnel (cloudflared) for local app sharing via node
  • QA/test automation hitting a temporary tunnel endpoint
  • curl-based health checks against a dev-hosted trycloudflare URL
  • PowerShell-based deployment script fetching from a partner's temporary tunnel
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName != "cloudflared.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "tunnel"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve which interpreter and command line contacted the tunnel; correlate with jquery.js execution (UC2) on the same host within minutes. 2) Contain: block the specific *.trycloudflare.com FQDN/IP at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and capture memory for module recovery. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts that resolved the same subdomain, extract resolved IPs as new IOCs, and check for follow-on credential exfiltration (UC4/UC5).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "trycloudflare.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe","mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery endswith "trycloudflare.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Djinn Stealer single-pass developer/cloud credential file sweep (incl. AI MCP configs) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts one non-developer process touching many distinct credential stores in a short window — AWS/cloud creds, SSH keys, Docker/Kube/Terraform/Vault, package-registry tokens (.npmrc, .pypirc, Cargo), and AI-assistant MCP configs like ~/.claude/mcp.json. Djinn collects 'in a single pass' all developer and infrastructure secrets, so breadth-of-access by a single process is the signal. Rationale: Builds directly on the article's enumerated target list — cloud creds, SSH keys, Docker/Helm/Terraform/Pulumi/Vault, npm/Yarn/pnpm/Cargo/Maven/Gradle/pip/NuGet tokens, and the distinctive AI-assistant MCP configs (~/.claude/mcp.json). The dcount>=5 threshold encodes Djinn's 'single pass' breadth and suppresses normal per-tool access. Datadog/Sigma omitted: this is a count/threshold detection and Datadog's listed auditd schema lacks a file-path field. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-critical-simplehelp-flaw-deploy-new-djinn-infostealer-taskweaver-malware/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup/sync agent (OneDrive, Dropbox, Backblaze) indexing the user home and touching dotfiles
  • Antivirus/EDR full-disk scan reading credential files
  • An IDE (non-Code) or shell-init reading many config files at session start
  • A developer onboarding script that copies multiple credential templates
  • Configuration-management agent (Ansible/Chef) reading secrets across stores
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe","backblaze.exe","ansible","chef-client")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess/SHA256 doing the sweep and whether it is signed/known; confirm it is not a backup or EDR scanner; check timing against jquery.js/trycloudflare events on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host and, per the article's guidance, treat all developer/cloud secrets on it as compromised — rotate AWS/cloud keys, SSH keys, GitHub/CLI tokens, package-registry tokens, Vault tokens, and revoke MCP/AI-assistant tokens. 3) Hunt: review cloud/SaaS audit logs for use of the stolen keys, look for a TAR+GZIP staging archive being created and exfiltrated, and check other developer endpoints for the same process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName has_any ("credentials","mcp.json","id_rsa","id_ed25519",".npmrc",".pypirc",".vault-token","config.json","hosts.yml")
   or FolderPath has_any (".aws",".ssh",".docker",".claude",".terraform","Pulumi",".kube",".config/gh")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","gh.exe","aws.exe","docker.exe","terraform.exe","kubectl.exe","code.exe","ssh.exe","ssh-agent.exe","Code.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctStores = dcount(FolderPath), Stores = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where DistinctStores >= 5
| order by DistinctStores desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.aws/","\\.aws\\","/.ssh/","\\.ssh\\","/.docker/","\\.docker\\",".npmrc",".pypirc","/.claude/","\\.claude\\","mcp.json",".vault-token",".terraform","Pulumi","/.config/gh/")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("git","gh","aws","docker","terraform","kubectl","code","ssh"))
| summarize DistinctStores = dcount(TargetFilePath), Stores = make_set(TargetFilePath, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId
| where DistinctStores >= 5
| order by DistinctStores desc

Djinn Stealer Linux /proc/<pid>/environ & cmdline secret harvesting AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single Linux process opening /proc/<pid>/environ and /proc/<pid>/cmdline across many PIDs to scrape secrets (API keys, tokens, credentials) from other processes' memory-backed virtual files. This is the distinctive Linux credential-access routine the article attributes to Djinn Stealer. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's Linux-specific behavior: 'reads the /proc/<pid>/cmdline and /proc/<pid>/environ virtual files that contain... secrets'. The >=20 distinct-PID threshold separates a stealer's enumeration from a debugger/monitoring tool inspecting one process. Defender/Datadog omitted: MDE-Linux and Datadog's listed auditd schema do not reliably surface /proc virtual-file reads with a path field; auditd-backed ImFileEvent/Falcon do. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-critical-simplehelp-flaw-deploy-new-djinn-infostealer-taskweaver-malware/
ATT&CKT1552 T1057
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Monitoring agents (node_exporter, Datadog agent, Sysdig) enumerating /proc for metrics
  • An APM/observability tool reading process environments
  • A sysadmin debugging with a script that walks /proc
  • Container runtime/security tooling inventorying process cmdlines
  • Backup or forensic tooling snapshotting process state
Suppression filter
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("datadog-agent","node_exporter","sysdig","falcon-sensor","prometheus")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process walking /proc and confirm it is not an approved monitoring/observability agent; capture its binary and hash. 2) Contain: isolate the host and rotate any credentials/tokens that were live in process environments (CI runners, app service accounts, API keys passed via env vars). 3) Hunt: correlate with the TaskWeaver loader (jquery.js) and trycloudflare C2 on the same host, and check for a TAR/GZIP exfil archive; sweep other Linux developer/build hosts for the same process name/hash.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/(environ|cmdline)"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("ps","top","htop","auditd","gdb","systemd","snapd","node_exporter")
| summarize ProcReads = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId
| where ProcReads >= 20
| order by ProcReads desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo | TargetFileName=/^\/proc\/\d+\/(environ|cmdline)$/i | NOT ContextImageFileName=/\/(ps|top|htop|auditd|gdb|systemd|snapd|node_exporter)$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=procReads)) | procReads >= 20

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48558")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48558")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
