Oracle E-Business Suite web tier (java/httpd) spawning a shell — CVE-2026-46817 post-exploit RCE AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of the unauthenticated File Transmission RCE in Oracle Payments (CVE-2026-46817): the EBS middle-tier process (WebLogic/Java or Oracle HTTP Server) spawning an OS shell, interpreter, or download utility. This is the web-shell / command-execution stage that follows a successful internet-facing exploit, independent of any specific request URI. Rationale: Anchors on the EBS web-tier process names (java/WebLogic/Oracle HTTP Server) as parent and shell/interpreter/download utilities as child — the generic post-RCE shape for CVE-2026-46817, which Oracle/Tenable confirm is an unauth File Transmission RCE. Avoids the unverified exploit URI returned by search. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/cspumay2026.html • https://www.tenable.com/plugins/nessus/318806 • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/oracle-ebusiness-suite-zero-day-exploitation
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EBS concurrent managers / AD utilities (adop, adstrtal, adstpall) legitimately invoking shell scripts from the Java tier
  • RMAN or backup jobs spawning shell from the Oracle stack
  • Monitoring/APM agents (e.g. OEM) executing OS commands via the app-tier user
  • Patch automation (adpatch/adop) calling perl and shell wrappers
  • DevOps deploy scripts running curl/wget from the WebLogic host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java","java.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("adop","adpatch","adstrtal","adstpall","adcmctl","FNDLIBR"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host — confirm the child shell's command line; benign EBS activity references adop/adpatch/concurrent-manager scripts, malicious activity shows recon (whoami/id/uname), curl/wget to external IPs, or interactive shells. 2) Contain: if the shell is unrecognized, isolate the EBS host from the network and snapshot it; preserve $INST_TOP/logs and Oracle HTTP Server access logs. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound connections from this host (esp. pubstorm[.]com/.net and any unfamiliar egress), look for new files under web-accessible OA_HTML/Payments dirs, and confirm CVE-2026-46817 patch (May 2026 CSPU) status across all EBS instances.

| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ksh","python","python3","perl","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","curl","wget","whoami","id","uname")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java","httpd","apache2","beasvc","weblogic")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","ksh","python","perl","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","curl","wget","whoami","uname")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Host communicating with Clop EBS extortion infrastructure (pubstorm[.]com / pubstorm[.]net) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects any internal host resolving or connecting to pubstorm.com or pubstorm.net, the CL0P (Clop) data-leak/extortion contact infrastructure tied to the Oracle E-Business Suite exploitation campaign. Mandiant/Google Cloud confirm these domains as CL0P DLS contact infrastructure, making any communication high-fidelity for a post-compromise EBS victim. Rationale: pubstorm.com/.net are second-source confirmed (Mandiant/Google Cloud) as CL0P extortion contact infrastructure for the Oracle EBS campaign; any resolution/connection from a corporate host is near-zero-FP and directly ties an EBS victim to the actor. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/oracle-ebusiness-suite-zero-day-exploitation • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-oracle-e-business-suite-flaw-now-exploited-in-attacks/

  • Threat-intel feed enrichment service performing passive DNS lookups
  • Email security gateway expanding links in quarantined extortion mail
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host + initiating process; confirm it's not a sanctioned TI/sandbox box. Treat any production EBS or finance host as a likely compromise. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block pubstorm.com/.net at the proxy/firewall/DNS sinkhole, and preserve volatile data. 3) Hunt: review the host for the CVE-2026-46817 web-tier→shell pattern (UC1), search mail flow for inbound/outbound mail to @pubstorm.com/.net (UC2-email), and audit recent large outbound transfers (data theft) from EBS application and database servers.

Inbound CL0P extortion email from pubstorm.com / pubstorm.net AIActions on Objectives High
Detects inbound email originating from the pubstorm.com or pubstorm.net domains — the CL0P contact addresses (support@pubstorm.com / support@pubstorm.net) used to deliver extortion demands to Oracle E-Business Suite data-theft victims. Receipt of such mail is a strong signal the organization has been breached and is being extorted. Rationale: support@pubstorm.com / support@pubstorm.net are Mandiant-confirmed CL0P extortion contact addresses on the CL0P DLS; an inbound message from these domains is a near-unambiguous post-breach extortion indicator for an EBS victim. Sigma/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty — mail-flow telemetry isn't expressible on those sources. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/oracle-ebusiness-suite-zero-day-exploitation • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-oracle-e-business-suite-flaw-now-exploited-in-attacks/

  • Threat-intel mailbox deliberately subscribed to actor comms for monitoring
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the message in the security portal, confirm true sender domain is pubstorm.com/.net (not a spoof), and capture recipients — extortion mail usually targets executives/finance. 2) Contain: do NOT engage the actor; preserve the email, invoke the IR/extortion playbook, and notify legal/leadership. Quarantine copies but retain forensic originals. 3) Hunt: correlate to EBS compromise evidence — UC1 (web-tier→shell), UC2 (pubstorm network beacons), CVE-2026-46817 exposure (UC4), and audit large outbound data transfers from EBS app/DB tiers in the weeks prior.

Internet-facing Oracle E-Business Suite hosts vulnerable to CVE-2026-46817 AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed hosts reporting the unpatched CVE-2026-46817 (Oracle Payments File Transmission unauth RCE, fixed in the May 2026 CSPU), prioritizing internet-facing instances. With active in-the-wild exploitation and ~450 EBS instances exposed online per Shadowserver, this is the exposure-reduction hunt that gets vulnerable systems patched before the web-tier→shell stage (UC1) ever fires. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE id (CVE-2026-46817) confirmed by Oracle's May 2026 CSPU and Tenable, joined to internet-facing status — the single most actionable response to an actively-exploited unauth RCE. Empty for Sigma/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch: vulnerability-inventory telemetry has no native shape there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/cspumay2026.html • https://www.tenable.com/plugins/nessus/318806 • https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2026-065/

Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the EBS version and whether the May 2026 CSPU is applied; prioritize rows where IsInternetFacing is true. 2) Contain: for exposed unpatched instances, apply the May 2026 CSPU immediately or, if patching must wait, restrict the File Transmission/Oracle Payments endpoint at the WAF/reverse proxy and limit inbound HTTP to known sources. 3) Hunt: on every exposed host, retro-hunt UC1 (web-tier→shell) and UC2 (pubstorm comms) over the available retention window to rule out prior compromise before patching closes the door.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Endpoint egress to named DCloud Uni-App crypto-scam / wallet-drainer domains · [LLM] Access to WhatsApp 'Security Help Center' lookalike credential-harvest domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Endpoint egress to named DCloud Uni-App crypto-scam / wallet-drainer domains AIDelivery High
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the specific second-level domains Infoblox tied to the DCloud Uni-App scam economy (fake exchanges, RainbowEx, LSSC scooter scam, wallet drainers). Article-specific because it pins to the concrete IOC set, not a generic 'newly registered domain' heuristic. Rationale: Uses the 20 concrete second-level domains pre-extracted from the article and confirmed against the Infoblox primary report; domain-exact matching keeps FP near zero. Cross-checked Infoblox blog, SecurityWeek, and GBHackers writeups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/from-san-pedro-to-salinas-how-a-chinese-framework-dcloud-uni-app-powers-a-global-scam-economy/ • https://www.securityweek.com/chinese-framework-powers-200000-scam-sites/ • https://gbhackers.com/dcloud-uni-app-framework/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst deliberately detonating the domains in a sandbox VM
  • SOAR/URL-detonation appliance auto-resolving the IOC during enrichment
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ that logs the query before blocking (appears as a 'hit' but was contained)
  • User following a news article link that embeds a screenshot host on one of the parked domains
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MpCmdRun.exe")) and not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","malware-vm"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting host/user and whether the resolution led to an actual TCP/443 connect (pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on same DeviceId ±2m); a sinkholed/blocked query is informational only. 2) Contain: if a live connection occurred, isolate the host, force a password reset for any crypto-exchange / WhatsApp / messaging accounts the user holds, and block the domain + resolved IP at proxy and DNS. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the full IOC domain set over 90d, pull browser history for invitation-code / deposit pages, and check for wallet-extension installs or seed-phrase entry on the device.
let scamDomains = dynamic(["whats-zwp.vip","faq-whatsapp-center.com","rainbowex.cc","nasdaqpro.top","futureblockchain.net","kirbycoco.cc","clintile.com","datashareclub.com","hkxiu.com","bepviews.com","lsscapp.com","lssc-canada.ca","lsscol.com","lssc.ltd","lightacer.com","ystl03106.top","ys904.top","aqy.dot02ig.cfd","xaai3xj.com","xaaitbb.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (scamDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let scamDomains = dynamic(["whats-zwp.vip","faq-whatsapp-center.com","rainbowex.cc","nasdaqpro.top","futureblockchain.net","kirbycoco.cc","clintile.com","datashareclub.com","hkxiu.com","bepviews.com","lsscapp.com","lssc-canada.ca","lsscol.com","lssc.ltd","lightacer.com","ystl03106.top","ys904.top","aqy.dot02ig.cfd","xaai3xj.com","xaaitbb.com"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (scamDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Access to WhatsApp 'Security Help Center' lookalike credential-harvest domains AIDelivery High
Hunts user devices reaching the WhatsApp-impersonation phishing domains in the DCloud campaign (whats-zwp.vip, faq-whatsapp-center.com) plus a lookalike heuristic for whats-*[.vip/.cfd/.top] domains, while excluding legitimate WhatsApp infrastructure. Targets the credential-harvest stage independently of the broader scam-domain list. Rationale: Anchored on the two concrete WhatsApp-impersonation domains named in the article and a tight whats-* lookalike regex with an explicit legitimate-WhatsApp allowlist; HKCERT independently issued a June 2026 alert on these fraudulent 'WhatsApp Security Centre' pages, corroborating the vector. Cross-checked against: • https://www.hkcert.org/security-bulletin/phishing-alert-beware-of-fraudulent-whatsapp-security-centre-pages-hijacking-accounts_20260612 • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/from-san-pedro-to-salinas-how-a-chinese-framework-dcloud-uni-app-powers-a-global-scam-economy/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WhatsApp Business API integrators using vanity subdomains that contain 'whats' (verify against the .com/.net allowlist)
  • Marketing/URL-shortener previews that include 'whatsapp' plus 'help' in a benign campaign landing path
  • Brand-protection / takedown vendor crawling the lookalike domains on the user's behalf
  • Internal awareness-training platform hosting a simulated WhatsApp phish on a whats-* test domain
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("whatsapp.com","whatsapp.net")) and not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and confirm a live HTTP(S) session to the lookalike host (not just a passive DNS hit); check UrlClickEvents to see if the link arrived via email/Teams and whether SafeLinks was bypassed. 2) Contain: reset the user's WhatsApp/messaging and any reused credentials, revoke active WhatsApp Web sessions, and block the domain + IP at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IP and ASN (e.g., CTG Server Limited AS152194 BPH) for sibling whats-* domains, sweep the org for other recipients of the same lure, and review for follow-on linked-device / account-takeover activity.
let legitWhatsApp = dynamic(["whatsapp.com","whatsapp.net"]);
let knownBad = dynamic(["whats-zwp.vip","faq-whatsapp-center.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend host = tolower(RemoteUrl)
| where host has_any (knownBad)
    or (host matches regex @"whats[\-_a-z0-9]+\.(vip|cfd|top|icu|xyz)")
    or (host has "whatsapp" and host has_any ("center","help","secur","verify"))
| where not(host endswith "whatsapp.com") and not(host endswith "whatsapp.net") and not(host has_any (legitWhatsApp) and host endswith "whatsapp.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let knownBad = dynamic(["whats-zwp.vip","faq-whatsapp-center.com"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(Url)
| extend host = tolower(tostring(parse_url(Url).Host))
| where host has_any (knownBad)
    or (host matches regex @"whats[\-_a-z0-9]+\.(vip|cfd|top|icu|xyz)")
    or (host has "whatsapp" and host has_any ("center","help","secur","verify"))
| where not(host endswith "whatsapp.com") and not(host endswith "whatsapp.net")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

Gamaredon Expands Ukraine Attacks with New Malware and Cloud Service Abuse

The Hacker News
2026-06-29 16 use cases 6 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A Russian advanced persistent threat (APT) group has continued to evolve and expand its malware arsenal as part of its ongoing cyber onslaught against Ukraine throughout 2025. Slovakian cybersecurity company ESET said it observed 35 distinct spear-phishing campaigns mounted by Gamaredon against new targets, with most of them taking place in the second half of the year. Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Gamaredon spear-phishing delivery via HTML-smuggling XHTML or archive attachment · [LLM] Gamaredon PteroLNK/PteroSetup weaponizing USB and network drives with LNK files · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gamaredon HTA downloader executed via mshta.exe from Startup/Temp · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gamaredon CVE-2025-8088 WinRAR ADS path traversal dropping payload into Startup folder · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Gamaredon PowerShell/HTA tools fetching C2 via dead-drop resolver cloud services · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Gamaredon CVE-2025-8088 WinRAR ADS path traversal dropping payload into Startup folder AIInstallation High
Hunts the Gamaredon-specific abuse of WinRAR path traversal (CVE-2025-8088, NTFS Alternate Data Stream traversal) to write its HTA downloader (or LNK/VBS) directly into the user's Startup folder during archive extraction, granting login persistence. Pivots on an archive tool writing an auto-executing file type outside the intended extraction directory. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete chain: WinRAR (CVE-2025-8088) writing the HTA downloader into the Windows Startup folder for next-login persistence. An archive extractor creating an auto-run file outside its own folder is the direct ADS-traversal artifact. Cross-checked ESET and NVD. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-8088 • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1203 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately extracting a portable app archive that places a real .exe/.lnk into Startup intentionally
  • Software installers shipped as RAR/7z self-extractors that add a legitimate startup entry
  • explorer.exe creating shortcuts in Startup when a user pins an app to run at login
  • Backup/sync tools restoring a Startup folder from an archive
  • IT-packaged onboarding archives that seed approved startup utilities
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" and FileName endswith ".lnk" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm WinRAR/Rar version on the host via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory — versions <7.13 are vulnerable; pull the dropped file's SHA256 and detonate/scan it; note if extension is .hta/.lnk. 2) Contain: isolate the host before next login (the Startup file auto-executes on logon), delete the Startup payload, and force WinRAR upgrade to 7.13+. 3) Hunt: search the same user/host for the source archive (email or USB origin), mshta.exe execution of the dropped HTA, and outbound traffic to dead-drop resolver domains.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe","7zFM.exe","explorer.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".lnk" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".cmd" or FileName endswith ".js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe","7zFM.exe","explorer.exe")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".hta" or TargetFileName endswith ".lnk" or TargetFileName endswith ".vbs" or TargetFileName endswith ".exe" or TargetFileName endswith ".cmd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Path Traversal Writing Autostart Payload to Startup Folder
id: 5f3c2a7e-9b41-4d8c-bb2e-7a1d6e9f0c12
description: Detects an archive utility writing an auto-executing file type into the user Startup folder, consistent with Gamaredon abuse of WinRAR ADS path traversal (CVE-2025-8088) for login persistence.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-8088
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/29
tags:
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.t1547.001
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
      - '\unrar.exe'
      - '\7zFM.exe'
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.hta'
      - '.lnk'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.exe'
      - '.cmd'
      - '.js'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\WinRAR.exe OR *\\winrar.exe OR *\\Rar.exe OR *\\rar.exe OR *\\UnRAR.exe OR *\\7zFM.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\\Startup\\* OR *\\startup\\*) @TargetFilename:(*.hta OR *.lnk OR *.vbs OR *.exe OR *.cmd OR *.js)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(winrar|rar|unrar|7zfm)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(hta|lnk|vbs|exe|cmd|js)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" (Filesystem.file_name="*.hta" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cmd" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.js") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe","7zFM.exe","explorer.exe","WinRAR.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Gamaredon spear-phishing delivery via HTML-smuggling XHTML or archive attachment AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Gamaredon initial-access vector: inbound spear-phishing mail delivering archive attachments (RAR/ZIP/7z) or XHTML/HTM files that use HTML smuggling to reconstruct a malicious HTA downloader client-side. Surfaces delivered messages carrying these attachment types so analysts can pivot to recipient-host execution. Rationale: Targets the article's stated delivery: 'archive attachments or XHTML files that employ HTML smuggling' to deliver HTA downloaders. The XHTML/HTM attachment type is the high-signal HTML-smuggling marker; archive types cover the alternate path. Sentinel/Falcon/Datadog left empty as inbound mail-attachment telemetry lives only in Defender for O365 (EmailAttachmentInfo) in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/f/old-winrar-flaw-fuels-attacks-on-ukraine.html
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1027.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate business RAR/ZIP/7z attachments (invoices, reports) from known partners
  • Marketing or newsletter mail with HTML/HTM body parts saved as attachments
  • Internal-to-external auto-forwarded archives misclassified as inbound
  • Developers exchanging .htm/.xhtml documentation files
  • Compressed log bundles sent to support inboxes
Response runbook
1) Triage: detonate the attachment SHA256 in a sandbox; for XHTML/HTM open it to confirm embedded base64 blob + JS Blob/anchor-download (HTML smuggling) reconstructing an HTA. 2) Contain: quarantine/soft-delete the message tenant-wide via EmailPostDeliveryEvents purge, block the sender domain, and check whether any recipient already opened it. 3) Hunt: on each recipient host, look for an HTA written to Temp/Startup and subsequent mshta.exe execution; check DeviceFileEvents for the smuggled HTA file write.
let SuspectExt = dynamic(["rar","zip","7z","xhtml","htm","html","hta"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | extend Ext = tolower(tostring(split(FileName, ".")[-1]))
    | where Ext in (SuspectExt)
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentName = FileName, Ext, FileType, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName, Ext, AttachmentSHA256, DeliveryAction
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let SuspectExt = dynamic(["rar","zip","7z","xhtml","htm","html","hta"]);
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | extend Ext = tolower(tostring(split(FileName, ".")[-1]))
    | where Ext in (SuspectExt)
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentName = FileName, Ext, FileType, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName, Ext, AttachmentSHA256, DeliveryAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Gamaredon HTA downloader executed via mshta.exe from Startup/Temp AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the Gamaredon HTA downloader by mshta.exe pointing at an .hta in the Startup, Temp, AppData or Public path (the auto-run persistence payload dropped via WinRAR/HTML smuggling), or mshta spawned by explorer/winrar/script hosts. This is the execution pivot that turns delivery+persistence into payload retrieval (e.g. PteroSand). Rationale: mshta.exe running a .hta out of Startup/Temp/AppData (or launched by explorer.exe on login, or by winrar.exe right after extraction) is the precise Gamaredon HTA-downloader execution step that drops PteroSand. Path + parent constraints keep it off generic mshta noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://gbhackers.com/winrar-cve-2025-8088-exploited/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that legitimately launch HTA UIs from AppData
  • Enterprise software using mshta for installer/help dialogs out of Temp
  • Admin scripts wrapping mshta for one-off automation
  • RMM/management agents invoking mshta from ProgramData
  • Browser/email clients caching an .htm to Temp opened by mshta during a benign workflow
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has @"\ProgramData\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full mshta command line and the HTA file contents/SHA256; confirm whether the HTA path is the Startup folder (persistence) and decode any inline javascript:/vbscript:. 2) Contain: kill the mshta process tree, isolate the host, and remove the HTA from Startup so it does not re-trigger on logon. 3) Hunt: follow the child processes (powershell.exe/wscript.exe) and outbound connections to dead-drop resolver services; pivot on the same SHA256 across the fleet and to the originating archive/email.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".hta", "javascript:", "vbscript:")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Startup\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
    or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where CommandLine has_any (".hta", "javascript:", "vbscript:")
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\Startup\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
    or ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\winrar.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon PowerShell/HTA tools fetching C2 via dead-drop resolver cloud services AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Gamaredon C2-resolution behaviour: scripting hosts (PowerShell, mshta, wscript, cscript, rundll32) reaching legitimate paste/blog/cloud-storage services used as dead-drop resolvers and payload hosts — Telegra.ph (PteroOdd), GoFile (PteroEffigy), Teletype, Rentry.co, Write.as, Paste.ee, Dropbox, Wasabi, Tebi. These services front the real C2 hidden behind tunnels/workers. Rationale: The article names the exact dead-drop resolver set (Telegra.ph→PteroOdd, GoFile→PteroEffigy, plus Teletype/Rentry/Write.as/Paste.ee/Dropbox/Wasabi/Tebi). A scripting host — not a browser — reaching these from a non-machine account is the high-fidelity C2-resolution signal. Sentinel uses DnsEvents (no per-process filter available on that table, so it is broader; pair with endpoint process telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://www.technadu.com/gamaredon-2025-new-tools-turla-alliance-cloud-exfiltration/629948/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/SREs running PowerShell scripts that legitimately pull artifacts from Dropbox or Wasabi/Tebi S3-compatible buckets
  • Automation using curl-via-powershell to fetch Gists/pastes for tooling
  • rundll32 in a benign app making telemetry calls that resolve a shared CDN
  • Technical writers' scripts posting to Dev.to/Telegra.ph APIs
  • Backup jobs reaching Wasabi/Dropbox object storage from scripted tasks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("choco","scoop","winget","\\Jenkins\\","azure-pipelines") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the script is downloading/parsing a paste (Invoke-WebRequest/DownloadString to telegra.ph/gofile) rather than a sanctioned dev workflow; extract any second-stage URL the dead drop returns. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the script process, and block the resolved C2 IP/tunnel domain at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: decode the dead-drop response for the real C2 (often behind *.workers.dev / DDNS / tunnels), and sweep the fleet for the same scripting-host→dead-drop pattern and for the upstream HTA/Startup persistence.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("telegra.ph","teletype.in","rentry.co","write.as","gofile.io","paste.ee","nopaste.net","dev.to","mastodon.social","tebi.io","wasabisys.com","dropbox.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("telegra.ph","teletype.in","rentry.co","write.as","gofile.io","paste.ee","nopaste.net","tebi.io","wasabisys.com","dropbox.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon PteroLNK/PteroSetup weaponizing USB and network drives with LNK files AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Gamaredon worming behaviour: a scripting host (wscript/cscript/powershell/mshta) creating malicious .lnk files on removable or mapped network drives (PteroLNK) to spread to other users and hosts. Scopes to file writes outside the system drive to surface USB/network-drive infection. Rationale: Targets PteroLNK/PteroSetup behaviour the article describes: infecting USB and network drives with malicious LNK files via script weaponizers. A script host writing .lnk files off the system drive (removable/mapped) is a rare, high-signal worming artifact; the count pivot catches bulk drive-wide seeding. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://web-assets.esetstatic.com/wls/en/papers/white-papers/gamaredon-in-2025.pdf
ATT&CKT1091 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Login scripts (cscript/wscript) deploying shortcut files to mapped home/share drives
  • Software deployment scripts creating app shortcuts on network shares
  • PowerShell DSC/GPO tooling provisioning Start Menu shortcuts to redirected folders
  • Backup or roaming-profile sync writing .lnk files to a network profile path
  • Admin maintenance scripts staging shortcuts on a USB toolkit drive
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\NETLOGON\\","\\SYSVOL\\","logon.vbs","Deploy-Application"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect one created .lnk target/arguments — Gamaredon LNKs invoke mshta/powershell to fetch a downloader; confirm the drive type (removable vs mapped) and the seeding script's command line. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block/remove the malicious LNKs from the affected share, and identify other hosts that mounted the same removable/network drive. 3) Hunt: search for the source weaponizer script (VBScript/PowerShell) and for execution of the dropped LNKs elsewhere, plus the downloader callbacks to dead-drop resolver services.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where not(FolderPath startswith "C:\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize LnkCount = count(), Paths = make_set(FolderPath, 20), arg_min(Timestamp, *) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LnkCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".lnk"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where not(TargetFilePath startswith "C:\\")
| summarize LnkCount = count(), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by LnkCount desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen network sniffing via netsh trace capture redirected to ADMIN$ share AIReconnaissance High
Hunts The Gentlemen's reconnaissance technique of running netsh trace packet capture and writing the .etl output across the network to a remote host's ADMIN$ share. The redirect of a netsh trace start/stop session to \\<ip>\ADMIN$\ is highly specific to this actor's credential-harvesting-from-the-wire workflow. Rationale: Built from the article's exact commands 'netsh trace start capture=yes report=no filemode=circular overwrite=yes maxSize=4 > \\<target IP>\ADMIN$\{RANDOM}' and the matching 'netsh trace stop' redirect. netsh trace + ADMIN$ redirect is rare in benign admin use, making this high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1040 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network engineer running netsh trace for legitimate troubleshooting and saving to a local file (no ADMIN$ redirect)
  • Endpoint support tooling that captures ETL traces locally
  • Microsoft support diagnostic scripts (TSS toolkit) invoking netsh trace
  • Vendor performance-monitoring agents starting circular ETW captures
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\TSS\\", "TSSv2") and AccountName endswith "admin")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the redirect target — a \\<remote-ip>\ADMIN$ path means cross-host write, not local troubleshooting. Identify the executing account and whether it is an admin/service account that does not normally run netsh. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the source host, reset the credentials of the executing account, and pull the dropped .etl from the target ADMIN$ share for analysis (it may contain cleartext creds). 3) HUNT: Search for SharpADWS/NetScan/Advanced IP Scanner activity, the deploy_gpo.ps1 script, and connections to 81.177.215.15:9443 on the same hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "netsh" and ProcessCommandLine has "trace"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("capture=yes", @"\ADMIN$\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has "netsh" and CommandLine has "trace"
| where CommandLine has_any ("capture=yes", "\\ADMIN$\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Netsh Trace Packet Capture Redirected to ADMIN$ Share (The Gentlemen)
id: 9b3a1f42-6c2e-4f0b-8d4a-2c7e51a9d3b1
description: Detects netsh trace network capture started/stopped with output redirected to a remote ADMIN$ share, a recon/sniffing technique used by The Gentlemen RaaS.

  - https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*netsh*" Processes.process="*trace*" (Processes.process="*capture=yes*" OR Processes.process="*ADMIN$*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
The Gentlemen Go backdoor C2 beacon to 81.177.215.15 on TCP/9443 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host establishing an outbound connection to the confirmed Gentlemen Go-backdoor C2 IP 81.177.215.15 on port 9443, the Yamux-multiplexed persistent channel used for remote command execution and SOCKS proxying. Single confirmed C2 indicator deployed a day before ransomware. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit C2 endpoint 81.177.215.15:9443 for the Yamux-based Go backdoor. A hardcoded malicious IP+port is a high-confidence, near-zero-FP network IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/ • https://s2w.inc/en/resource/detail/1053
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers/sandbox detonating the sample from corporate ranges
  • Threat-intel scanning or Shodan-style internet measurement hitting the IP
  • Reused VPS IP later assigned to a benign service (validate against current TI reputation)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — a Go binary in an unusual path (Temp/Public/AppData) deployed ~1 day prior is the backdoor. Capture its SHA256 against the article's hash list. 2) CONTAIN: Network-isolate the host, block 81.177.215.15 at the perimeter, and kill/quarantine the implant binary. 3) HUNT: Look for WMI query 'SELECT UUID FROM Win32_ComputerSystemProduct', cmd.exe /c children of the implant (operator command 'c'), SOCKS proxy listeners, and expect ransomware staging within ~24h.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "81.177.215.15" and RemotePort == 9443
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "81.177.215.15" and DstPortNumber == 9443
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen BYOVD vulnerable driver drop/load (EDR-killer drivers) AIInstallation High
Hunts for the specific vulnerable kernel drivers The Gentlemen abuse in their BYOVD/GentleKiller workflow to terminate security products. Matches on the named .sys files being written or loaded, e.g. biontdrv.sys, wamsdk.sys, ProcessMonitorDriver.sys. Rationale: Driver names taken verbatim from the article's vulnerable-driver table (Safetica, WatchDog, Paragon biontdrv, inpoutx64, etc.). ESET's GentleKiller research corroborates these as the actor's BYOVD arsenal. Medium FP because inpoutx64.sys/biontdrv.sys also appear in legitimate software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • inpoutx64.sys loaded by legitimate RGB-lighting/overclocking utilities
  • biontdrv.sys present from a genuine Paragon Partition Manager install
  • gamedriverx64.sys from a legitimately installed game with anti-cheat
  • Security product (Safetica) itself loading ProcessMonitorDriver.sys in an authorized deployment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","paragon.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Check the signing status and the parent process that wrote/loaded the driver — a driver dropped to a non-standard path by a non-installer process is malicious; a vendor MSI installer is likely benign. Confirm whether the matching legitimate product is actually installed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, stop the driver service, and quarantine the .sys + the loading process; verify EDR/AV agents are still running. 3) HUNT: Correlate with Set-MpPreference tampering, OpenArk64/PowerRun.exe execution, and the 81.177.215.15 C2 on the same host to confirm Gentlemen activity.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ProcessMonitorDriver.sys","wamsdk.sys","gamedriverx64.sys","biontdrv.sys","inpoutx64.sys","wsftprm.sys","Havoc.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("ProcessMonitorDriver.sys","wamsdk.sys","gamedriverx64.sys","biontdrv.sys","inpoutx64.sys","wsftprm.sys","Havoc.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen impair defenses via Set-MpPreference exclusions and AV-removal tooling AIInstallation High
Detects The Gentlemen's defense-evasion step that disables Defender real-time/CFA protection, adds whole-drive exclusions via Set-MpPreference/Add-MpPreference, and runs known AV-removal utilities (kavrmvr.exe, OpenArk64, PowerRun.exe, Allpatch2.exe). Pairs the Go-implant PowerShell cmdlets with named tampering binaries. Rationale: Combines the article's verbatim Go-implant cmdlets (Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring, -EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled, Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess/-ExclusionPath 'C:\') with named tools kavrmvr.exe (Kaspersky uninstaller) and OpenArk64; PowerRun.exe/Allpatch2.exe added from corroborating Trend Micro reporting on the same actor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately adding a Defender exclusion for a line-of-business app (single ExclusionPath, not C:\)
  • Sanctioned migration off Kaspersky running kavrmvr.exe with change-ticket approval
  • Performance team disabling Real-Time Monitoring temporarily during a benchmark
  • Software packaging/SCCM scripts setting exclusions for an installer
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath" and ProcessCommandLine !has @"'C:\'" and ProcessCommandLine !has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the exclusion scope — a whole-drive 'C:\' exclusion or DisableRealtimeMonitoring chained with ExclusionProcess is malicious; a narrow app path may be benign. Identify the parent process (Go implant / cmd.exe /c). 2) CONTAIN: Re-enable Defender real-time protection and CFA, remove rogue exclusions, isolate the host, and reset the executing account. 3) HUNT: Pivot to BYOVD driver loads, registry Defender-policy keys, deploy_gpo.ps1, and the 81.177.215.15 C2 to scope the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("kavrmvr.exe","OpenArk64.exe","PowerRun.exe","Allpatch2.exe"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
        and ProcessCommandLine has "MpPreference"
        and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionPath"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName has_any ("kavrmvr.exe","OpenArk64.exe","PowerRun.exe","Allpatch2.exe"))
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
        and CommandLine has "MpPreference"
        and CommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionPath"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
