The Gentlemen Windows Defender disabled via Policy registry keys AIInstallation High
Detects The Gentlemen disabling Defender by writing the policy registry values DisableAntiSpyware / DisableBehaviorMonitoring / DisableOnAccessProtection / DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable = 1 under the Windows Defender policy hive (via .reg import). Distinct registry-telemetry pivot from the PowerShell-based tampering. Rationale: Registry keys and values are taken verbatim from the article's exported .reg block under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender. Value-name + data=1 under the policy hive is high-fidelity tampering. Falcon left empty: these policy keys are not reliably captured by the AsepValueUpdate (autostart) event the FDR exposes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps • https://s2w.inc/en/resource/detail/1053
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Group Policy legitimately disabling Defender on hosts managed by a third-party AV (DisableAntiSpyware pushed by GPO)
  • Gold-image build process turning off Defender before installing the enterprise AV
  • Admin troubleshooting an AV conflict by temporarily setting DisableBehaviorMonitoring
  • MDM/SCCM baseline applying a Defender configuration
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","svchost.exe","ccmexec.exe","WmiPrvSE.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether a sanctioned GPO/MDM pushed the value (InitiatingProcess = svchost/gpscript) versus an interactive process like reg.exe/regedit/cmd.exe run by a user. Check if a different enterprise AV is the intended owner. 2) CONTAIN: Revert the registry values, force a gpupdate, isolate the host if the writer was interactive/non-admin. 3) HUNT: Correlate same-host BYOVD driver loads, Set-MpPreference tampering, and C2 to 81.177.215.15:9443; expect ransomware staging shortly after.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("DisableAntiSpyware","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableOnAccessProtection","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable")
| where RegistryValueData == "1"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("DisableAntiSpyware","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableOnAccessProtection","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable")
| where RegistryValueData in ("1","0x1","DWORD (0x00000001)")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen ransomware deployment via deploy_gpo.ps1 / NETLOGON staging AIActions on Objectives High
Detects The Gentlemen's domain-wide lateral movement: execution of the custom deploy_gpo.ps1 GPO-deployment script and staging of the ransomware executable on the NETLOGON share for simultaneous distribution to domain hosts. Rationale: Uses the article's named lateral-movement script deploy_gpo.ps1 and the NETLOGON-share distribution method. The deploy_gpo.ps1 filename is unique to this actor; NETLOGON-staged .exe execution corroborated by SOC Prime and Trend Micro GPO-abuse reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://socprime.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-detection/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
ATT&CKT1484.001 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate logon-script .exe staged in NETLOGON (e.g. drive-mapping or inventory tool) executed at user logon
  • AD admin running a sanctioned GPO-deployment PowerShell script with a different name (excluded by deploy_gpo.ps1 specificity)
  • Software-distribution tooling that copies installers into SYSVOL/NETLOGON
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has @"\NETLOGON\" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("userinit.exe","gpscript.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("logon.exe","mapdrives","inventory"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open deploy_gpo.ps1 / the NETLOGON-staged binary and hash it against the article's ransomware MD5 list; identify the privileged account and source DC that staged it. 2) CONTAIN: Remove the malicious GPO and the NETLOGON/SYSVOL payload immediately, disable the abused account, and block the ransomware hash org-wide before logon-driven execution spreads. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all hosts that pulled the NETLOGON object, check for PsExec-based execution of the same binary, BYOVD driver loads, and shadow-copy deletion as pre-encryption signals.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "deploy_gpo.ps1"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has @"\NETLOGON\" and ProcessCommandLine has ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has "deploy_gpo.ps1"
    or (CommandLine has "\\NETLOGON\\" and CommandLine has ".exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),

| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)

| order by conn_count desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Your inbox is an identity system all of its own: whoever owns it may own a lot more

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Microsoft Removes 119 Edge Extensions That Hid Malware in Images and Fonts

The Hacker News
2026-06-29 11 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft has shut down a long-running malicious extension operation on the Edge Add-ons store that hid its payloads inside ordinary image and font files, then woke up days after install to steal credentials and run ad fraud. The company calls it&nbsp;StegoAd, a mash-up of steganography and adware, and ties 119 extensions to a single threat actor it says has been active since at least 2021.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1176 T1190 T1204.002 T1219 T1528
Domainsmitarchive.info liveupdt.com dealctr.com ipaglov.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] StegoAd/DarkSpectre Edge-extension C2 beacon to liveupdt.com / dealctr.com · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] StegoAd credential/cookie exfiltration to mitarchive.info (DarkSpectre) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
StegoAd/DarkSpectre Edge-extension C2 beacon to liveupdt.com / dealctr.com AICommand & Control High
Hunts host contact with the StegoAd ad-fraud command-and-control domains liveupdt.com and dealctr.com, the C2 cluster Microsoft attributes to the 119 malicious Edge extensions and Koi Security ties to DarkSpectre (ShadyPanda/GhostPoster). Because these domains are dedicated malicious infrastructure, any resolution or connection from a managed host indicates a live StegoAd-family extension calling home. Rationale: liveupdt.com and dealctr.com are the shared ShadyPanda/GhostPoster/StegoAd C2 domains confirmed by both Microsoft's StegoAd report and Koi Security's DarkSpectre write-up — dedicated malicious infrastructure, so domain contact alone is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/darkspectre-unmasking-the-threat-actor-behind-7-8-million-infected-browsers • https://thehackernews.com/2025/12/darkspectre-browser-extension-campaigns.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment platform or passive-DNS collector resolving the IOC domains for research
  • SOC malware-analysis sandbox VM detonating a sample that beacons to these domains
  • DNS sinkhole / RPZ that resolves the domain to an internal blackhole IP (still logs the query)
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation tooling pre-resolving flagged domains
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the initiating process (expect msedge.exe/chrome.exe/firefox.exe). Open edge://extensions on the host and compare installed add-on IDs against Microsoft's StegoAd technical-report list. 2) Contain: isolate the host or block the domains at egress/DNS; remove the offending extension and clear browser-stored cookies/sessions. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for contact with mitarchive.info/gmzdaily.com (credential exfil) and force password resets + revoke sessions for Google/WordPress/banking accounts used on that host; prefer hardware-key MFA.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("liveupdt.com", "dealctr.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("liveupdt.com", "dealctr.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: StegoAd/DarkSpectre C2 Domain Resolution (liveupdt.com / dealctr.com)

StegoAd credential/cookie exfiltration to mitarchive.info (DarkSpectre) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts host contact with mitarchive.info (and the linked gmzdaily.com), the exfiltration endpoint Microsoft observed receiving stolen Google credentials, 2FA codes, WordPress logins and bulk session cookies from the StegoAd extensions. Koi Security ties mitarchive.info specifically to the DarkSpectre credential-theft payload, making any contact a credible account-takeover precursor. Rationale: mitarchive.info is named in the article as the StegoAd credential-exfil domain and is independently attributed to DarkSpectre's credential payload by Koi Security; gmzdaily.com is the linked second exfil domain from Koi's research — both are dedicated malicious endpoints, so contact strongly implies stolen cookies/credentials in transit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/darkspectre-unmasking-the-threat-actor-behind-7-8-million-infected-browsers • https://thehackernews.com/2025/12/darkspectre-browser-extension-campaigns.html
ATT&CKT1539 T1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Passive-DNS / threat-intel platform resolving the IOC for enrichment
  • Analyst sandbox detonating a StegoAd sample under controlled conditions
  • DNS RPZ/sinkhole logging the query while redirecting to a blackhole address
  • Brand-protection or takedown service probing the actor domain
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which host/user and which browser process resolved the domain; treat the browser profile as compromised. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block mitarchive.info/gmzdaily.com at DNS+egress, remove the malicious extension, and immediately revoke active sessions and force password resets for Google, WordPress and any sensitive accounts used on that host. 3) Hunt: pivot the same DeviceId/user to liveupdt.com/dealctr.com C2 contact, review Entra/Google sign-in activity for anomalous IPs post-exfil, and recommend hardware-key MFA over SMS to defeat the 2FA-code theft.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("mitarchive.info", "gmzdaily.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("mitarchive.info", "gmzdaily.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

status: experimental

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Critical

Public PoC Released for Critical libssh2 CVE-2026-55200 Client-Side SSH Flaw

The Hacker News
2026-06-29 9 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A public proof-of-concept is now out for CVE-2026-55200, a critical flaw in libssh2 that lets a malicious or compromised SSH server trigger memory corruption on a connecting client, with possible code execution. No credentials, no user interaction. The bug affects every release up to and including 1.11.1 and carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. libssh2 is a client-side SSH library, not a server.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] libssh2-carrier client (curl/Git/PHP) making outbound SSH to an external server · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable libssh2 exposure inventory (CVE-2026-55200 / 55199 / 2025-15661) · [LLM] Client crash with faulting module libssh2 (CVE-2026-55200 exploitation fallout) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

libssh2-carrier client (curl/Git/PHP) making outbound SSH to an external server AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the precondition for CVE-2026-55200 exploitation: a process that statically or dynamically links libssh2 (curl.exe, git.exe, php.exe/php-cgi.exe) opening an outbound TCP/22 SSH session to a public, non-corporate endpoint. A malicious or compromised SSH server triggers the client-side heap overflow during the handshake, so the connection itself is the attack surface the article tells defenders to prioritize. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named libssh2 carriers (curl, Git, PHP) plus port 22 and a public destination — the exact 'clients that reach external SSH servers' the advisory says to prioritize. Cross-checked against GHSA-r8mh-x5qv-7gg2 and the NHS England alert which list the same carriers. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r8mh-x5qv-7gg2 • https://digital.nhs.uk/cyber-alerts/2026/cc-4799 • https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q2/1014
ATT&CKT1203
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate CI/CD pipelines using curl/git over SCP/SFTP to external code or artifact hosts
  • PHP applications with the ssh2 extension syncing to a partner SFTP server
  • Developer workstations cloning/pushing to git over SSH to GitHub/GitLab (often via OpenSSH, but git over libssh2 transports exist)
  • Backup or firmware-update agents reaching vendor SSH endpoints on TCP/22
  • Internal jump-host SSH that resolves to a public-facing NAT address
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith "github.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith "gitlab.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith "bitbucket.org"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve the RemoteIP/DstHost — is it a known partner SFTP/git host or an unfamiliar internet endpoint? Check whether the initiating curl/php/git binary and any bundled libssh2.dll are at or below 1.11.1 (lacking commit 97acf3d). Step 2 (contain): If the endpoint is unknown/untrusted, block the outbound TCP/22 to that IP at the egress firewall and isolate the host pending review; SSH from automation should only hit allow-listed servers. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same host for an immediate process crash of the carrier binary (UC: faulting module libssh2) and for any child process spawned by curl/php/git right after the connection, which would indicate successful code execution.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 22
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl.exe","git.exe","php.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), RemoteEndpoints=make_set(strcat(RemoteIP,":",tostring(RemotePort)),50), Cmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 22
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Sessions=count(), DstHosts=make_set(DstHostname,50) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc

Vulnerable libssh2 exposure inventory (CVE-2026-55200 / 55199 / 2025-15661) AIExploitation High
Surfaces every managed device where Defender TVM has identified a libssh2-linked package vulnerable to the batch disclosed June 2026 — the unauthenticated heap-overflow CVE-2026-55200 plus the companion DoS (CVE-2026-55199) and SFTP heap over-read (CVE-2025-15661). Used to drive backport/patch prioritization since no tagged libssh2 release exists yet. Rationale: Pivots on the three exact CVE IDs the article enumerates for the libssh2 batch; TVM is the cleanest way to find the curl/Git/PHP/appliance copies. Note (cross-checked against the article and GHSA-r8mh-x5qv-7gg2): statically-linked/bundled copies that package managers do not register will NOT appear here, so this is a floor not a ceiling on exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r8mh-x5qv-7gg2 • https://digital.nhs.uk/cyber-alerts/2026/cc-4799
ATT&CKT1203
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM lag: a device already backported to commit 97acf3d may still report vulnerable until the next scan reconciles the build string
  • Vendor appliances reporting a libssh2 version string but with a vendor backport applied (false positive on version match)
  • Decommissioned/offline assets still present in the inventory snapshot
  • End-of-life images flagged but isolated and not reaching external SSH
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Sort by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel and cross-reference each device's libssh2 version against 1.11.1; confirm whether the installed build already carries commit 97acf3d (distro backports often keep the 1.11.1 version string). Step 2 (contain): For unpatched internet-reaching clients, restrict outbound SSH to trusted/allow-listed servers and enforce host-key verification until a patched build lands. Step 3 (hunt): For each vulnerable host, run UC1 to see if it has actually made outbound TCP/22 to an external endpoint, and manually enumerate statically-linked copies (backup agents, firmware updaters) that TVM cannot see.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-55200","CVE-2026-55199","CVE-2025-15661")
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where SoftwareName has "libssh2" | project DeviceName, SoftwareName, InventoryVersion=SoftwareVersion) on DeviceName
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-55200","CVE-2026-55199","CVE-2025-15661")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceName, CveId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel desc
Client crash with faulting module libssh2 (CVE-2026-55200 exploitation fallout) AIExploitation Medium
Detects Windows Application Error (Event ID 1000) where the faulting module or application is libssh2 or one of its carriers (curl/git/php), the expected symptom of the CVE-2026-55200 out-of-bounds heap write when a connecting client parses an oversized SSH packet. The article explicitly says to watch for 'unexplained client crashes.' Rationale: The exploit primitive is an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-680) confirmed in GHSA-r8mh-x5qv-7gg2; a non-clean exploit attempt crashes the carrier with libssh2 as the faulting module — a high-fidelity, article-named symptom ('unexplained client crashes'). Defender XDR has no native WER/Application-Error table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; this lands on Sentinel Event / Splunk WinEventLog / Sigma application channel. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r8mh-x5qv-7gg2 • https://digital.nhs.uk/cyber-alerts/2026/cc-4799
ATT&CKT1203
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine non-malicious bug or version mismatch crashing curl/php with libssh2 against a benign but misconfigured SSH/SFTP server
  • Memory-pressure / OOM crashes of php-cgi under load that happen to fault in libssh2
  • Faulty appliance firmware-update agent crashing on a flaky network handshake
  • Developer-tool crashes during normal git-over-SSH operations unrelated to the CVE
Suppression filter
| where RenderedDescription has "0xc0000005" or RenderedDescription has "libssh2"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full Event 1000 record — confirm the faulting module is libssh2(.dll) or a statically-linked carrier and capture the exception code (0xC0000005 access violation strongly supports memory corruption). Correlate against UC1 for an outbound TCP/22 connection from the same host/process in the seconds before the crash. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and block egress to the SSH server it last connected to; preserve any crash dump for reverse-engineering. Step 3 (hunt): Look for a child process or new persistence spawned by the carrier immediately before/after the crash (successful RCE), and sweep other hosts running the same vulnerable libssh2 build (UC2) for matching crashes.
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventLog == "Application"
| where Source == "Application Error" and EventID == 1000
| where RenderedDescription has "libssh2"
    or RenderedDescription has_any ("curl.exe","git.exe","php.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Source, EventID, RenderedDescription
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VS Code/Cursor folder-open task auto-runs Node against fake .woff2 font (Fake Font / Contagious Interview) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Stage-1 trigger of the 'Fake Font' supply-chain attack: a hidden .vscode/tasks.json task (eslint-check, runOn:folderOpen) that launches node.exe against public/fonts/fa-solid-400.woff2, a font file that actually contains XOR/eval JavaScript. Node executing a .woff2 has no legitimate use, making this the highest-fidelity initial-access pivot. Rationale: node.exe with a .woff2 in its command line is the campaign's exact Stage-1 invocation (JFrog confirms task 'eslint-check'/runOn:folderOpen runs Node against public/fonts/fa-solid-400.woff2); font files are never legitimately interpreted by Node, so this is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://opensourcemalware.com/blog/how-malware-abuses-npm-lifecycle-scripts-and-vs-code-tasks • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1052/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately bundling/optimizing webfonts with a custom Node build script that happens to read .woff2 paths (would not match fa-solid-400.woff2 + execute-as-code shape)
  • Font-subsetting tooling (e.g. fontmin/subset-font) invoked via node passing .woff2 as an input argument
  • Internal tooling that validates font assets by path
  • CI build agents running font pipelines (filter by interactive user / non-build host)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("fontmin","subset-font","ttf2woff","glyphhanger") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: Open the matched node.exe command line and confirm the .woff2 is being executed as code, not read as an asset; inspect the project's .vscode/tasks.json for a task named 'eslint-check' with runOn:'folderOpen' and hide:true. 2) Contain: Kill the node process tree, isolate the developer host, and quarantine the project folder; block child node -e processes. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the same host for outbound connections to api.trongrid.io / aptoslabs / bsc RPC and to C2 IPs 166.88.134.62, 198.105.127.210, 23.27.202.27, and for a python install under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Python\Python3127.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".woff2"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "fa-solid-400.woff2" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\public\fonts\" or ProcessCommandLine has "/public/fonts/"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".woff2"
| where CommandLine has "fa-solid-400.woff2" or CommandLine has "\\public\\fonts\\" or CommandLine has "/public/fonts/"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js process resolves blockchain dead-drop (TronGrid/Aptos/BSC RPC) — Fake Font Stage-2 C2 retrieval AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the campaign's takedown-resilient dead-drop resolver: the fake font loader queries TronGrid, falls back to Aptos, then BSC JSON-RPC to extract an encrypted next stage from transaction input. A node.exe (or a detached node -e) reaching these specific blockchain RPC endpoints right after project open is highly anomalous for a normal build process. Rationale: JFrog confirms the loader resolves stages from api.trongrid.io (primary), fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com (fallback), then bsc-dataseed.binance.org / bsc-rpc.publicnode.com; scoping the initiator to node/Code/Cursor removes generic web3 dev noise while keeping the campaign's exact infra. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine web3/blockchain developers whose node project legitimately queries TronGrid/BSC RPC during dApp testing
  • A Hardhat/Truffle/ethers.js test suite hitting bsc-dataseed for fork testing
  • Wallet or DEX tooling run from VS Code's integrated terminal
  • Browser extensions proxied through node dev servers querying the same RPC
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("web3-dev-01","blockchain-build-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the host has no legitimate blockchain/dApp project; check whether the node process was spawned by a folder-open task and whether a .woff2 was just executed. 2) Contain: Isolate host; block the four RPC FQDNs at egress only for non-web3 user populations and kill the node tree. 3) Hunt: Look on the same host for follow-on connections to C2 IPs (166.88.134.62/198.105.127.210/23.27.202.27) and downloads of /d/python.zip or /d/7zr.exe.
DeviceNetworkEvents

Fake Font socket.io C2 — connections to hardcoded IPs and /$/boot //snv //d/python.zip endpoints AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Stage-3 socket.io backdoor and tool-download channel: node.exe beaconing to the three hardcoded C2 IPs or requesting the campaign's distinctive URI paths (/$/boot, /snv, /verify-human, /d/python.zip, /d/7zr.exe). Hard attacker infrastructure plus unique endpoint shapes make this alerting-grade. Rationale: The three IPs and the /$/boot, /snv, /verify-human, /d/python.zip|7z, /d/7zr.exe endpoints are JFrog-documented attacker C2/tool-download infrastructure — hardcoded IOCs with no benign use, making IP-match alerting-safe and the URI paths a strong proxy-log corroborator. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://intel.breakglass.tech/post/invisibleferret-contagious-interview-dprk-lazarus-kimsuky-crossover

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic

  • IP reuse after the documented infrastructure is sinkholed/reassigned (validate against current threat-intel feed before alerting long after publication)
  • A security researcher or sandbox detonating the sample from a corporate host
  • Proxy-path matches on unrelated apps that coincidentally use /snv or /boot (constrained here by node/Code/Cursor initiator in Defender)
  • Threat-intel scanning infrastructure probing the same IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm direction is outbound from a developer endpoint and the initiating process is node/Code/Cursor; pull the matched URI paths from proxy logs. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, block all three IPs at the egress firewall, and revoke the developer's session tokens. 3) Hunt: Search for the preceding folder-open node execution, blockchain RPC lookups, and a subsequent python install under Python3127, then begin credential-rotation for all secrets reachable from that host.

Fake Font Stage-4 Python toolchain staging — node drops python.zip/7zr.exe/get-pip.py into .npm AIInstallation High
Hunts the install stage where the loader downloads a private Python runtime and 7-Zip (/d/python.zip, /d/7zr.exe), bootstraps pip via /tmp/get-pip.py, and unpacks Python to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Python\Python3127. File writes of these named artifacts by node.exe into the .npm staging directory are a tight, article-specific signal. Rationale: JFrog documents node fetching /d/python.zip, /d/7zr.exe and /tmp/get-pip.py and unpacking to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Python\Python3127; a Node process writing a bundled Python+7zip toolchain into the npm cache dir is never legitimate and uniquely fingerprints this loader. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A node-based installer (e.g. an Electron app build) that legitimately bundles a portable Python — rare and usually not written under ~/.npm
  • Developer manually downloading get-pip.py for offline pip bootstrap (different parent than node.exe)
  • node-gyp or node-sass historically invoking Python (invokes python.exe, does not drop python.zip/7zr.exe)
  • CI cache warmers populating .npm with package tarballs (no python.zip/7zr.exe filenames)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("electron-builder","node-gyp") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the writing process is node.exe and the drop path is the npm cache (.npm) or a non-standard Python3127 dir; hash python.zip/7zr.exe and check reputation. 2) Contain: Isolate host, kill node and any spawned python under Python3127, and quarantine the staging directory. 3) Hunt: Look for the subsequent python.exe reading GitHub CLI hosts.yml / browser Login Data and creating a ZIP under %USERPROFILE%\.npm, plus exfil to the C2 IPs or a Telegram bot.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("python.zip","python.7z","7zr.exe","get-pip.py")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe" or FolderPath has @"\.npm\" or FolderPath has "/.npm/" or FolderPath has @"\Programs\Python\Python3127"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("python.zip","python.7z","7zr.exe","get-pip.py")
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe" or TargetFilePath has "\\.npm\\" or TargetFilePath has "/.npm/" or TargetFilePath has "Python3127"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

InvisibleFerret stealer — Python harvests dev creds/wallets and stages ZIP into .npm exfil dir AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Stage-5 InvisibleFerret infostealer: a freshly-installed Python interpreter reads developer/credential artifacts (GitHub CLI hosts.yml, browser Login Data, wallet extensions) and packages loot into a compressed archive under %USERPROFILE%\.npm (Windows) or /tmp/.npm (Linux/macOS) for upload to C2/Telegram. Python writing a ZIP into the npm cache is the cleanest collection/staging signal. Rationale: JFrog confirms InvisibleFerret stages collected credentials/wallets into compressed archives under %USERPROFILE%\.npm (Win) and /tmp/.npm (Linux/macOS) before C2/Telegram upload; python.exe writing a .zip/.7z into the npm cache dir is a tight collection-stage IOC, with hosts.yml/Login Data/globalStorage as corroborating access targets. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://intel.breakglass.tech/post/invisibleferret-contagious-interview-dprk-lazarus-kimsuky-crossover
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.001 T1555.003 T1560
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Python build/packaging script (e.g. an npm postinstall calling python) legitimately writing a .zip into the project's node_modules — distinct from the user-profile .npm cache
  • Developer test fixtures that zip artifacts into a temp .npm path
  • Backup tooling archiving the npm cache directory (different parent than python.exe)
  • node-gyp builds invoking python that emit build artifacts (not .zip in ~/.npm)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","setup.py bdist","pip wheel") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the python.exe parent traces back to the Python3127 loader / node folder-open chain and that the archive sits in the user-profile .npm dir; list the archive contents if recoverable. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, kill python, and block egress to the C2 IPs and api.telegram.org; preserve the archive for IR. 3) Hunt: Treat all credentials reachable from the host as compromised — rotate Git/GitHub tokens (hosts.yml), browser-stored passwords, cloud API keys and crypto wallet seeds immediately, and sweep the org for the other Fake Font stages.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "python.exe"
| where (FolderPath has @"\.npm\" or FolderPath has "/.npm/") and (FileName endswith ".zip" or FileName endswith ".7z")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hosts.yml",@"\Login Data","globalStorage","Local State")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has "python.exe"
| where (TargetFilePath has "\\.npm\\" or TargetFilePath has "/.npm/") and (TargetFileName endswith ".zip" or TargetFileName endswith ".7z")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
