title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

FBI Warns Russian Intelligence Hackers Target Signal Backup Recovery Keys

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-06-26 10 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The FBI and CISA have updated&nbsp;their March warning&nbsp;about Russian intelligence phishing Signal accounts, and the operators have added a step: they now coax targets into handing over their Signal Backup Recovery Key. Hand it over once, and the attacker can restore the account's backup, read the private and group message history, and take over the account. Worse, the key keeps working.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound email impersonating Signal support requesting Backup Recovery Key / device-link (UNC4221) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Signal Desktop linked-device URI (sgnl://linkdevice) invoked from a clicked link (UNC5792) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Signal Desktop linked-device URI (sgnl://linkdevice) invoked from a clicked link (UNC5792) AIInstallation High
Hunts the actual account-takeover mechanism in the FBI/CISA UNC5792 campaign: a doctored 'group invite' link hands the Signal custom-scheme URI sgnl://linkdevice?uuid= to the registered protocol handler, spawning Signal Desktop with that URI on its command line and linking an attacker device. Legitimate device linking is done via in-app QR scan, so a clicked sgnl://linkdevice URL is anomalous and high-fidelity. Rationale: Grounded in the GTIG-confirmed device-linking URI 'sgnl://linkdevice?uuid=' (the exact JS payload GTIG documented for UNC5792's doctored Signal group-invite pages) — the article only describes this as 'doctored group invite links that silently linked an attacker's device.' Matching the static URI prefix on the process command line is high-fidelity because legitimate linking is QR-based, never a clicked URL handler. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/russia-targeting-signal-messenger/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-phishing-campaigns-exploit-signals-device-linking-feature/ • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260626
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1098.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user genuinely re-linking Signal Desktop by clicking a 'link device' deep link rather than scanning the QR (uncommon but possible)
  • Security-awareness phishing simulation or red-team exercise reproducing the UNC5792 device-link lure
  • Clipboard managers or note apps that echo/log a copied sgnl:// URI into a launched process
  • Signal Desktop self-initiated relink/update flows that regenerate a sgnl:// URI internally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe","outlook.exe","teams.exe","ms-teams.exe","olk.exe")  // keep only externally-triggered handoffs; legit in-app relink has Signal.exe / explorer.exe as parent
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the InitiatingProcessFileName (parent). A browser, Outlook, or Teams parent handing off sgnl://linkdevice is the phishing-click pattern; a Signal.exe self-parent is more likely benign relinking. Confirm with the user whether they were asked by 'Signal support' to link a device. 2) CONTAIN: Have the user open Signal > Settings > Linked Devices and remove any unrecognized device immediately, then rotate their Backup Recovery Key (Settings > Backups) to invalidate the attacker's archive access; consider the account and prior backups compromised. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same user/device for inbound 'Signal support' lures, other endpoints where the same recipient clicked the invite, and any DeviceNetworkEvents to newly-seen domains around the link-click time.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "sgnl://linkdevice"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "sgnl://linkdevice"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Signal Desktop Linked-Device URI Invocation (UNC5792)
id: 6f3a1c84-9b27-4d51-bc0e-3a7e9f2d18b4
description: Detects Signal Desktop being launched with the sgnl://linkdevice device-linking URI on the command line, the device-takeover step abused by UNC5792/UNC4221 via doctored group-invite links. Legitimate linking uses in-app QR scanning, not a clicked URL handler.
references:
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/russia-targeting-signal-messenger/
  - https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260626
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/27
tags:
  - attack.t1204.001
  - attack.t1098.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains: 'sgnl://linkdevice'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - User legitimately re-linking Signal Desktop via a deep link
  - Red-team or security-awareness testing of the Signal linking flow
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:(*sgnl://linkdevice* OR *SGNL://LINKDEVICE*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/sgnl:\/\/linkdevice/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*sgnl://linkdevice*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*sgnl://linkdevice*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Inbound email impersonating Signal support requesting Backup Recovery Key / device-link (UNC4221) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the delivery phase where the UNC5792/UNC4221 'Signal support' lure reaches the enterprise via email rather than in-app: messages impersonating Signal that instruct the recipient to enable backups and surrender their Recovery Key, or to add a linked device. Uses the IC3 PSA's verbatim lure language as the anchor. Rationale: Anchored on verbatim lure strings published in IC3 PSA I-062626 ('Action Required: Data Recovery Needed', 'View Recovery Key', 'connection of third-party devices') combined with Signal sender-impersonation. The advisory states the primary channel is in-app, so this is scoped as a hunting-tier catch for email-delivered variants of the same UNC4221 lure that actually transit enterprise mail. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260626 • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/russia-targeting-signal-messenger/
ATT&CKT1598.003 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Signal Foundation / signal.org transactional or newsletter email mentioning backups or linked devices
  • Internal security-awareness phishing simulation reusing the Signal recovery-key lure
  • IT/helpdesk notifications to staff about enabling backups or removing linked devices
  • User-to-user mail where the sender display name happens to contain 'Signal'
  • Vendor security bulletins forwarded internally that quote the FBI/CISA advisory text
Suppression filter
| where not (SenderMailFromDomain in~ ("signal.org","account.signal.org","signal.foundation"))  // exclude genuine Signal Foundation senders; keep look-alike/impersonating domains
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm direction is inbound and the sender is external; validate SPF/DKIM/DMARC via AuthenticationDetails and check whether the sending domain is a Signal look-alike. Pull any URLs via EmailUrlInfo and detonate/inspect for a sgnl://linkdevice redirect. 2) CONTAIN: If malicious, soft-delete/quarantine the message tenant-wide (purge by NetworkMessageId), block the sender domain, and notify recipients not to paste any Recovery Key, PIN, or code. 3) HUNT: Correlate recipients against the companion endpoint detection (sgnl://linkdevice process invocation) to see who proceeded to link a device, and sweep for the same subject/sender across the last 30 days.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where (SenderDisplayName has "Signal" or SenderFromDomain has "signal")
| where Subject has_any ("Recovery Key","Data Recovery Needed","Backup Recovery","third-party devices","linked device","Action Required")
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderDisplayName,
          SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, UrlCount
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where (SenderDisplayName has "Signal" or SenderFromDomain has "signal")
| where Subject has_any ("Recovery Key","Data Recovery Needed","Backup Recovery","third-party devices","linked device","Action Required")
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderDisplayName,
          SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, UrlCount
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.direction="inbound" (All_Email.subject="*Recovery Key*" OR All_Email.subject="*Data Recovery Needed*" OR All_Email.subject="*Backup Recovery*" OR All_Email.subject="*third-party devices*" OR All_Email.subject="*linked device*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.direction="inbound" (All_Email.subject="*Recovery Key*" OR All_Email.subject="*Data Recovery Needed*" OR All_Email.subject="*Backup Recovery*" OR All_Email.subject="*third-party devices*" OR All_Email.subject="*linked device*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA sets urgent deadline to fix Cisco flaw exploited in attacks

BleepingComputer
2026-06-26 6 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is giving federal agencies until Sunday to patch a vulnerability in Cisco Unified Communications Manager Server that is being actively exploited. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Cisco Unified CM SSRF webshell deployment via WebDialer to /platform-services/axis2-web/ (CVE-2026-20230)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] KEV exposure inventory: CISA BOD 26-04 assets carrying CVE-2026-20230 / CVE-2026-12569 · [LLM] PTC Windchill Tomcat/Java process spawning OS command shell (RCE command execution)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PTC Windchill JSP webshell drop ([0-9a-f]{16}.jsp under codebase/login)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PTC Windchill webshell interaction: POST to /Windchill/login/[16hex].jsp or X-windchill-req header
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
KEV exposure inventory: CISA BOD 26-04 assets carrying CVE-2026-20230 / CVE-2026-12569 AIExploitation High
Surfaces every managed asset in the estate whose vulnerability inventory reports the two CISA KEV CVEs with the June 28 patch deadline (Cisco Unified CM SSRF and PTC Windchill/FlexPLM deserialization RCE). This is the exposure-management pivot that drives the urgent remediation mandate rather than detecting attacker activity. Rationale: Uses the two exact KEV CVE IDs named in the article (CVE-2026-20230, CVE-2026-12569) against the vuln-inventory tables; a clean exposure list driving the BOD 26-04 June 28 deadline, zero hallucinated values. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/csa/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW.html • https://www.ptc.com/en/about/trust-center/advisory-center/active-advisories/windchill-flexplm-rce-vulnerability • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-12569
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Asset already patched but scanner snapshot is stale (scan predates remediation)
  • Decommissioned CUCM/Windchill host still in CMDB but powered off
  • Vuln scanner version-detection false positive on a back-ported vendor hotfix
  • Lab/test Windchill instance intentionally left unpatched for validation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm each returned host is internet-reachable and, for CUCM, whether WebDialer is enabled (disabled by default — its absence sharply lowers CVE-2026-20230 risk). Step 2 (contain): For exposed hosts that cannot be patched before June 28, apply vendor mitigations — disable WebDialer on CUCM, apply PTC's Apache/IIS rewrite workaround on Windchill, or restrict ingress to the management VLAN. Step 3 (hunt): For every unpatched host, immediately run the webshell-drop and webshell-access UCs (below) against the same asset to determine whether exploitation already occurred before patching.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-20230", "CVE-2026-12569")
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-20230", "CVE-2026-12569")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Vulnerabilities where (Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2026-20230","CVE-2026-12569")) by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.signature Vulnerabilities.cve Vulnerabilities.severity | drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities) | sort 0 dest
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Vulnerabilities where (Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2026-20230","CVE-2026-12569")) by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.signature Vulnerabilities.cve Vulnerabilities.severity | drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities) | sort 0 dest
PTC Windchill JSP webshell drop ([0-9a-f]{16}.jsp under codebase/login) AIInstallation High
Detects the persistent JSP webshell that CVE-2026-12569 exploitation drops into the Windchill login directory — files named with exactly 16 lowercase hex characters written under a Windchill codebase/login path. This is the install-stage artifact confirmed across PTC, CISA and multiple vendor write-ups of the active campaign. Rationale: Anchors on the campaign's confirmed webshell naming convention — exactly 16 lowercase hex chars (.jsp/.jspx) under .../Windchill/codebase/login/ — reported by PTC and multiple vendors; the random-hex name + login-path combo has no legitimate Windchill equivalent, making it very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ptc.com/en/about/trust-center/advisory-center/active-advisories/windchill-flexplm-rce-vulnerability • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/cisa-adds-exploited-ptc-windchill-rce.html • https://www.securityweek.com/first-ever-exploitation-of-ptc-windchill-vulnerability-discovered-in-the-wild/amp/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windchill cumulative patch deployment writing JSPs (named descriptively, not 16-hex random — will not match the regex)
  • Backup/restore of the codebase directory replaying historical JSPs
  • Security-team validation drop during purple-team testing of this exact IOC
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the dropped file's SHA256 and contents; confirm it is a JSP webshell (runtime command exec, X-windchill-req header handling) and note the writing process (should be the Tomcat/java process). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the Windchill host, quarantine the JSP, and block the source IP at the perimeter; preserve Tomcat access logs before rotation. Step 3 (hunt): Search web logs for POST requests to /Windchill/login/[0-9a-f]{16}.jsp (webshell-access UC) to find every shell name and the operator IPs, and check for child shells spawned from java.exe on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "Windchill" and FolderPath has "login"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{16}\.jspx?$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRename")
| where TargetFilePath has "Windchill" and TargetFilePath has "login"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{16}\.jspx?$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: PTC Windchill JSP Webshell Dropped in codebase/login (CVE-2026-12569)
id: 8f3c1d2e-6a4b-4c11-9d77-2b5e0a9f1c44
description: Detects creation of a 16-hex-character JSP/JSPX file under a Windchill login/codebase directory, the persistent webshell artifact of CVE-2026-12569 exploitation.
references:
  - https://www.ptc.com/en/about/trust-center/advisory-center/active-advisories/windchill-flexplm-rce-vulnerability
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/cisa-adds-exploited-ptc-windchill-rce.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/27
tags:
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Windchill\'
  selection_login:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\login\'
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|re: '(?i)\\[0-9a-f]{16}\.jspx?$'
  condition: all of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate Windchill patch/deploy writing JSPs (will not match the 16-hex random name)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\Windchill\\* OR *\\windchill\\*) AND @TargetFilename:(*\\login\\* OR *\\codebase\\*)) @TargetFilename:(*.jsp OR *.jspx OR *.JSP)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\Windchill\\.*\\login\\[0-9a-f]{16}\.jspx?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*Windchill*login*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*codebase*login*") (Filesystem.file_name="*.jsp" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.jspx") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem) | regex file_name="(?i)^[0-9a-f]{16}\.jspx?$" | convert ctime(firstTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*Windchill*login*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*codebase*login*") (Filesystem.file_name="*.jsp" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.jspx") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem) | regex file_name="(?i)^[0-9a-f]{16}\.jspx?$" | convert ctime(firstTime)
PTC Windchill webshell interaction: POST to /Windchill/login/[16hex].jsp or X-windchill-req header AICommand & Control High
Detects HTTP interaction with the CVE-2026-12569 JSP webshells — POST requests to /Windchill/login/<16-hex>.jsp, a path that legitimate Windchill traffic never POSTs to, and the attacker-specific X-windchill-req control header. Runs against web/proxy/WAF telemetry fronting the Windchill server. Rationale: Uses two confirmed, no-legitimate-use IOCs from PTC/vendor reporting: POST to /Windchill/login/[0-9a-f]{16}.jsp (legit Windchill never POSTs there) and the X-windchill-req control header — both campaign-specific, not a generic webshell template. Defender left empty: webshell HTTP interaction with the Windchill appliance lives in proxy/WAF logs, not endpoint EDR tables. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ptc.com/en/about/trust-center/advisory-center/active-advisories/windchill-flexplm-rce-vulnerability • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/cisa-adds-exploited-ptc-windchill-rce.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Tenable/Qualys) replaying the public PoC against the Windchill host during a sanctioned scan window
  • Internal red-team validating the IOC
  • WAF that URL-decodes and double-logs the same request (dedup on SourceIP+RequestURL)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the SourceIP and the exact JSP name hit; correlate to the file-drop UC to confirm the shell exists on disk. Treat any 200-response POST to this path as confirmed interactive compromise. Step 2 (contain): Block the SourceIP at the WAF/perimeter, isolate the Windchill host, and revoke any Windchill service/app credentials that could have been harvested. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate ALL distinct /Windchill/login/*.jsp names seen across web logs (shells are renamed per deployment), pull request bodies for X-windchill-req command selectors to reconstruct operator actions, and pivot on the SourceIP across other internet-facing assets.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DestinationServiceName has "Windchill" or RequestURL has "/Windchill/"
| where (RequestMethod == "POST" and RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)/Windchill/login/[0-9a-f]{16}\.jsp")
      or (RequestContext has "X-windchill-req")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: PTC Windchill Webshell HTTP Interaction (CVE-2026-12569)
id: 3d9a7c54-1f8b-49e2-bb0a-7c6d4e2f9011
description: Detects POST requests to a 16-hex-named JSP under /Windchill/login/, the webshell-access pattern of CVE-2026-12569. Legitimate Windchill traffic never POSTs to /Windchill/login/*.jsp.
references:
  - https://www.ptc.com/en/about/trust-center/advisory-center/active-advisories/windchill-flexplm-rce-vulnerability
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ptc-warns-of-imminent-threat-from-critical-windchill-flexplm-rce-bug/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/27
tags:
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-method: 'POST'
    cs-uri-stem|re: '(?i)/Windchill/login/[0-9a-f]{16}\.jsp'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - None expected; Windchill does not POST to /Windchill/login/*.jsp legitimately
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" Web.url="*/Windchill/login/*.jsp" by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_host Web.url Web.http_method Web.status Web.http_user_agent | drop_dm_object_name(Web) | regex url="(?i)/Windchill/login/[0-9a-f]{16}\.jsp" | convert ctime(firstTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" Web.url="*/Windchill/login/*.jsp" by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_host Web.url Web.http_method Web.status Web.http_user_agent | drop_dm_object_name(Web) | regex url="(?i)/Windchill/login/[0-9a-f]{16}\.jsp" | convert ctime(firstTime)
PTC Windchill Tomcat/Java process spawning OS command shell (RCE command execution) AIExploitation High
Detects the Windchill/FlexPLM application server (Apache Tomcat / java.exe) spawning a Windows command interpreter or recon utility — the on-host execution that follows CVE-2026-12569 deserialization RCE and JSP-webshell command handling. A Java app-server spawning cmd/powershell is anomalous and high-signal. Rationale: Pairs the article/advisory-confirmed Windchill Tomcat-Java app-server context (path contains Windchill/ptc/FlexPLM) as parent with command-shell/recon children — a parent+child combination, not a bare process filter; a Java PLM server legitimately almost never spawns cmd/powershell, so the pivot is high-fidelity for post-RCE command execution. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ptc.com/en/about/trust-center/advisory-center/active-advisories/windchill-flexplm-rce-vulnerability • https://kudelskisecurity.com/research/critical-rce-vulnerability-in-windchill-and-flexplm • https://securityaffairs.com/190049/security/cisa-and-bsi-warn-orgs-of-critical-ptc-windchill-and-flexplm-flaw.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windchill install/upgrade or hotfix scripts that legitimately shell out (correlate to a change-management window)
  • Monitoring/backup agents launched by the Tomcat service account
  • Admin running diagnostic batch jobs under the Windchill service context
  • Java-based scheduled task invoking net.exe for share mapping
Suppression filter
// Suppress known maintenance contexts
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "installer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "upgrade"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "Veeam" and ProcessCommandLine !has "backup"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for recon (whoami/systeminfo/ipconfig), credential or download activity (certutil/bitsadmin), and confirm the parent java path is the Windchill/FlexPLM instance — rule out a scheduled change window. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, suspend the Windchill Tomcat service, and capture memory/process tree before remediation. Step 3 (hunt): Run the JSP-drop and webshell-access UCs on the same host to find the entry webshell, review the full process tree under java.exe for follow-on tooling, and check for outbound connections from the recon children.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe", "javaw.exe", "tomcat9.exe", "tomcat10.exe", "tomcat11.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("Windchill", "ptc", "FlexPLM")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "powershell_ise.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "whoami.exe", "systeminfo.exe", "ipconfig.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ParentImg = tolower(ParentProcessName), ChildImg = tolower(NewProcessName)
| where ParentImg has_any ("java.exe", "javaw.exe", "tomcat9.exe", "tomcat10.exe", "tomcat11.exe")
| where ParentImg has_any ("windchill", "ptc", "flexplm")
| where ChildImg has_any ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "net.exe", "whoami.exe", "systeminfo.exe", "ipconfig.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Unified CM SSRF webshell deployment via WebDialer to /platform-services/axis2-web/ (CVE-2026-20230) AIDelivery Medium
Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-20230, where the WebDialer SSRF is abused to stand up a rogue Apache Axis service and write first/second-stage JSP shells under /platform-services/axis2-web/ on Cisco Unified CM. Runs against WAF/reverse-proxy and Web access logs fronting the CUCM appliance (which itself rarely carries EDR). Rationale: Anchors on the confirmed CVE-2026-20230 attack chain from Cisco PSIRT and Help Net Security: WebDialer SSRF -> rogue Apache Axis -> JSP shell under /platform-services/axis2-web/. That path is the second-source-validated webshell location. Defender/Falcon left empty because CUCM is a hardened Linux appliance with no endpoint EDR — the only realistic telemetry is the fronting WAF/proxy/load-balancer Web logs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/csa/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/24/cisco-unified-cm-flaw-exploited-to-drop-webshells-cve-2026-20230/ • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-20230/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner replaying the public CVE-2026-20230 PoC against CUCM during a sanctioned window
  • Cisco TAC/professional-services diagnostic accessing platform-services during a support case
  • Internal red-team validation of the axis2-web IOC
  • WAF double-logging the same request after URL normalization (dedup on SourceIP+RequestURL)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether WebDialer is enabled on the targeted CUCM (disabled by default — if off, exploitation is unlikely); identify the SourceIP (campaign uses Tor) and whether any axis2-web request returned 200. Step 2 (contain): Disable WebDialer, block the SourceIP, and restrict CUCM web ingress to trusted management ranges; engage Cisco TAC to inspect /platform-services/axis2-web/ on the appliance filesystem for planted JSPs. Step 3 (hunt): Review CUCM CLI/audit and proxy logs for follow-on command-exec shell access and privilege-escalation-to-root activity, and check whether the same Tor/source IPs touched other internet-facing Cisco appliances.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has "/platform-services/axis2-web/" or RequestURL has "/webdialer/"
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("CUCM", "CallManager", "Unified") or DestinationServiceName has_any ("cucm", "callmanager")
      or RequestURL has "/platform-services/axis2-web/"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-26 11 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Exploitation. Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single source IP producing a high volume of failed authentications against a Fortinet appliance (SSL-VPN / admin login) followed by a successful login in the same window — the exact 'successful logins shortly after large-volume password failure events' pattern Unit 42 flags for the FortiBleed credential-spraying campaign. Rationale: Implements Unit 42's explicit FortiBleed guidance — audit remote-access logs for successful logins shortly after large-volume failure events — scoped to Fortinet auth via the CIM app values / DeviceVendor='Fortinet'. Threshold + same-window success join is what separates spray-then-compromise from routine VPN typos. Cross-checked with SOCRadar/SecurityWeek FortiBleed reporting and Arctic Wolf's CVE-2024-55591 analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.004 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote worker repeatedly fat-fingering an SSL-VPN password then succeeding
  • Misconfigured VPN client or saved-credential loop retrying stale creds before a successful re-auth
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Tenable) credential checks against the appliance
  • Shared NAT egress IP where many staff log in (inflated failure+success counts from one SourceIP)
  • Password-rotation day causing widespread first-attempt failures followed by success
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<populate watchlist: known scanner + corp NAT egress IPs via a Sentinel watchlist join, not inline>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CompromisedUser + SourceIP; geolocate SourceIP and check whether the success used MFA and from a known ASN/country. Inspect the failed-user set — many distinct users from one IP = spray, not a typo. 2) Contain: if SourceIP is foreign/unrecognized, force-disable the compromised admin/VPN account, kill active SSL-VPN tunnels, block the SourceIP at the edge, and rotate the credential. 3) Hunt: from that SourceIP/account pivot to post-auth config changes (new admin accounts, sslvpn user groups), jsconsole admin logins, and any config download — feed into the FortiBleed jsconsole and rogue-admin UCs.
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 1h;
let Failed = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("failure","failed") or Message has_any ("login failed","Login failed","authentication failed","ssl-login-fail"))
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetUsers = dcount(DestinationHostName) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
let Success = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("success","succeeded") or Message has_any ("login successful","SSL tunnel established"))
| summarize Successes = count(), CompromisedUser = make_set(DestinationHostName, 20) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
Failed
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 = empirical spray burst floor per source per hour
| join kind=inner Success on SourceIP, TimeGenerated
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, Failures, TargetUsers, Successes, CompromisedUser
| order by Failures desc

FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) AIExploitation High
Hunts the high-fidelity exploitation signature of CVE-2024-55591: administrative logins attributed to the 'jsconsole' interface and/or successful super-admin logins sourced from the device loopback/local IP — the artifact the Node.js websocket auth-bypass leaves when an unauthenticated attacker forges super_admin access on FortiOS/FortiProxy. Rationale: Uses the two corroborated CVE-2024-55591 exploitation artifacts — `ui=jsconsole` in the admin-login record (matched in CommonSecurityLog Message) and super-admin logins from the device loopback/local IP (CIM Authentication.src=127.0.0.1) — reported by Arctic Wolf, watchTowr ('I Am The Super_Admin Now') and Trustwave. Both are near-zero in benign FortiGate operation. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://labs.watchtowr.com/get-fortirekt-i-am-the-super_admin-now-fortios-authentication-bypass-cve-2024-55591/ • https://trustwave.com/en-us/resources/blogs/spiderlabs-blog/cve-2024-55591-fortinet-fortios-fortiproxy-zero-day
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001 T1556
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately running CLI commands through the FortiGate GUI 'CLI console' widget (also tagged jsconsole) — distinguish by source being a real admin IP, not loopback
  • Automation/orchestration tooling (Ansible/FortiManager) driving CLI via the local console
  • Internal penetration test replicating CVE-2024-55591
  • Health-check scripts hitting the management interface from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the jsconsole/loopback login corresponds to a real admin session — legitimate jsconsole use originates from an authenticated GUI session with a genuine admin SourceIP; exploitation shows loopback/local src and no preceding interactive auth. Check FortiOS version against the CVE-2024-55591 fixed builds. 2) Contain: isolate the device's management interface from the internet, disable/rotate all admin accounts, and capture the running + startup config for IR. 3) Hunt: enumerate admin accounts and sslvpn user groups created/modified after the first jsconsole login, look for `--userfrom`-style audit-record tampering, and any config download/exfil to chain with the rogue-admin and FortiBleed config-extraction UCs.

| where Message has_any ("login","logged in","logged-in","admin")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, DeviceExternalID, SourceIP, AdminUser = SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, Activity, EventOutcome, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit AIInstallation High
Hunts post-exploitation persistence for the FortiBleed/CVE-2024-55591 chain: creation of new FortiGate administrator accounts (often random usernames) or new SSL-VPN local users / user groups via config changes. This is how attackers convert a one-shot auth bypass into durable, high-privilege access for offline-cracked credential re-use. Rationale: Targets the documented CVE-2024-55591 post-exploit actions — new admin accounts with random names, new SSL-VPN local users and groups — via Fortinet config-change logs (cfgpath system.admin / user.group) and the CIM Change datamodel (action=created, object_category=user). Account creation on an edge appliance is rare and tightly change-controlled, so FP is low. Corroborated by Arctic Wolf and Cyble. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://cyble.com/blog/cve-2024-55591-the-fortinet-flaw-putting-critical-systems-at-risk/
ATT&CKT1136 T1098 T1133
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned admin onboarding by the network team during a change window
  • FortiManager/automation pushing a config template that provisions admin or VPN users
  • Legitimate SSL-VPN user-group expansion during an access-request rollout
  • MSP/managed-SOC provisioning a monitoring admin account
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ActorAdmin and SourceIP that created the new object; correlate against an authorized change ticket and verify the actor session was not a jsconsole/loopback exploit login. Flag random-looking usernames. 2) Contain: delete or disable the unauthorized admin/VPN account and group, terminate its sessions, and rotate credentials for every legitimate admin on the device. 3) Hunt: review whether the new account granted VPN access, established tunnels into internal networks, or downloaded the device config; pivot on its SourceIP across other edge devices to scope the FortiBleed campaign footprint.

| where Message has_any ("system.admin","user.local","user.group")
| where Message has_any ("super_admin","prof_admin","accprofile","sslvpn")
| where Message has_any ("Object attribute configured","Added","cfgattr","New","create")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, ActorAdmin = SourceUserName, NewObject = DestinationHostName, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the FortiBleed campaign's parallel targeting of internet-exposed MSSQL: a single client IP generating a burst of SQL Server login failures (error 18456) across one or many logins within a short window — the spray signature Unit 42 observed against MSSQL devices alongside Fortinet and Sophos. Rationale: Covers the article's explicit observation that the FortiBleed actors also targeted MSSQL devices. Pivots on SQL Server error 18456 (login failed) parsed for CLIENT IP and login name in Sentinel's Event table, with a Defender DeviceLogonEvents fallback for Windows-auth brute force against the SQL host and a CIM Authentication path for Splunk. Threshold-based, so framed as a burst detector. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application/service account with a stale connection string hammering the DB after a password change
  • Linked-server or ETL job misconfigured with wrong credentials retrying in a tight loop
  • Monitoring agent (SCOM/SolarWinds) probing SQL with expired creds
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner credential audit against the SQL instance
  • Developer load-test pointing at the wrong SQL host
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("sqlmonitor","svc-etl","svc-backup")   // tune to your known SQL service accounts
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve ClientIP — internal app server vs external/unknown. Inspect the targeted login set: many distinct logins from one IP = spray; a single service account = likely stale credential. Check for any 18454/successful login from the same ClientIP right after the burst. 2) Contain: if external, block the ClientIP at the firewall, confirm the SQL instance is not directly internet-exposed, and disable SQL-auth logins that were sprayed; enforce that MSSQL sits behind the VPN/jump box. 3) Hunt: if a success followed, review that login's subsequent activity (xp_cmdshell, new SQL logins, linked-server abuse) and pivot the ClientIP across Fortinet edge logs to tie it to the broader FortiBleed spraying infrastructure.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| where LogonType in ("Network","Batch")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedAccounts = dcount(AccountName), Accounts = make_set(AccountName, 30), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 failed network logons / 30 min from one source = spray
| order by Failures desc
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 30m;
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Source == "MSSQLSERVER"
| where EventID == 18456   // SQL Server: Login failed
| extend LoginUser = extract(@"Login failed for user '([^']+)'", 1, RenderedDescription)
| extend ClientIP = extract(@"\[CLIENT: ([0-9A-Fa-f\.:]+)\]", 1, RenderedDescription)
| where isnotempty(ClientIP)
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedLogins = dcount(LoginUser), Logins = make_set(LoginUser, 30) by ClientIP, Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where Failures >= 30
| order by Failures desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("mssqlserver","mssql","sqlserver","microsoft sql server") Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.src, Authentication.user, _time span=30m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(count) as failures, dc(user) as targeted_logins, values(user) as logins by src, _time

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      tool exclusion list per environment.

New SharkLoader Malware Deploys Cobalt Strike in StrikeShark Cyberattacks

The Hacker News
2026-06-26 20 use cases 8 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A newly discovered cyber attack campaign has been observed delivering a previously undocumented malware family called SharkLoader that acts as a loader for deploying Cobalt Strike Beacon on compromised hosts. Kaspersky, which is tracking the activity under the moniker StrikeShark, said the campaign has targeted a diplomatic organization in Indonesia, government organizations in Taiwan,

SharkLoader DLL side-load: SystemSettings.exe loads malicious SystemSettings.dll AIInstallation High
Hunts the StrikeShark loader's core execution primitive: the legitimate Windows binary SystemSettings.exe loading a SystemSettings.dll that does NOT live in System32/WinSxS. The genuine DLL only ever loads from the OS directory, so a copy in any user/temp/app path is the SharkLoader side-load. Rationale: Uses the article's exact side-load pair (SystemSettings.exe + SystemSettings.dll) anchored on the location anomaly — the legit DLL is OS-resident only, so any other path is the loader. Cross-checked vs Securelist and cybersecuritynews write-ups confirming the SystemSettings.exe→SystemSettings.dll chain. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1574.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft-signed Settings app components running from a servicing staging directory during a feature update
  • Third-party software that legitimately ships a file named SystemSettings.exe in its own program directory (rare, investigate signer)
  • Application virtualization/sandbox tools (App-V, MSIX) that reflect OS binaries into virtualized paths
  • Forensic/IR tooling that copies system binaries to an evidence folder and executes them
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\WindowsApps\" and FolderPath !has @"\Program Files\WindowsApps\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256/MD5 of the loaded SystemSettings.dll and the parent path; check signer (legit DLL is Microsoft-signed and in System32) and submit hash to the IOC list below. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host and suspend/kill the SystemSettings.exe process tree; preserve memory for the in-thread Cobalt Strike beacon. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for DscCoreR.mui / SyncRes.dat file writes, Run-key/scheduled-task references to SystemSettings.exe, and outbound to connect-microsoft.com / ms-record.com / ms-record.top / ms-tray.top.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "SystemSettings.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SystemSettings.exe"
| where FolderPath !has @"\Windows\System32\" and FolderPath !has @"\Windows\SysWOW64\" and FolderPath !has @"\Windows\WinSxS\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\SystemSettings.exe"
| where NewProcessName !has "\\Windows\\System32\\" and NewProcessName !has "\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\" and NewProcessName !has "\\Windows\\WinSxS\\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharkLoader encrypted component drop: DscCoreR.mui / SyncRes.dat written to disk AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the two SharkLoader payload modules — DscCoreR.mui (compressed Cobalt Strike Beacon + MinHook) and SyncRes.dat (Detours API-hook stager). Both filenames are SharkLoader-specific and not standard Windows resources, making any write a high-fidelity loader-staging signal. Rationale: DscCoreR.mui and SyncRes.dat are unique SharkLoader artifact names confirmed across Securelist and helpnetsecurity; neither is a real Windows MUI/DAT resource, so a write is near-zero-FP staging evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/26/sharkloader-dropper-governments-software-developers/
ATT&CKT1105 T1027.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Backup/restore software re-hydrating a previously infected host's files
  • An analyst copying captured IOC samples onto a sandbox VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe", "SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) — expect SystemSettings.exe or a dropper masquerading as Google Update / Cisco AnyConnect; hash the dropped files. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory before reboot (beacon lives in an injected suspended thread). 3) Hunt: pivot to the parent process tree, look for the SystemSettings.exe side-load, and search the org for the same SHA256 of DscCoreR.mui/SyncRes.dat.

| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| order by TimeGenerated desc
